A Meta Logarithmic-Sobolev Inequality for Phase-Covariant Gaussian Channels

Salman Beigi Affiliation: 1School of Mathematics, Institute for Research in Fundamental Sciences (IPM), P.O. Box 19395-5746, Tehran, Iran
2Centre for Quantum Technologies, National University of Singapore, Singapore
3School of Physics, Institute for Research in Fundamental Sciences (IPM), P.O. Box 19395-5531, Tehran, Iran    Saleh Rahimi-Keshari Affiliation: 1School of Mathematics, Institute for Research in Fundamental Sciences (IPM), P.O. Box 19395-5746, Tehran, Iran
2Centre for Quantum Technologies, National University of Singapore, Singapore
3School of Physics, Institute for Research in Fundamental Sciences (IPM), P.O. Box 19395-5531, Tehran, Iran
Abstract

We introduce a meta logarithmic-Sobolev (log-Sobolev) inequality for the Lindbladian of all single-mode phase-covariant Gaussian channels of bosonic quantum systems, and prove that this inequality is saturated by thermal states. We show that our inequality provides a general framework to derive information theoretic results regarding phase-covariant Gaussian channels. Specifically, by using the optimality of thermal states, we explicitly compute the optimal constant αp\alpha_{p}, for 1≤p≤21\leq p\leq 2, of the pp-log-Sobolev inequality associated to the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup. Prior to our work, the optimal constant was only determined for p=1p=1. Our meta log-Sobolev inequality also enables us to provide an alternative proof for the constrained minimum output entropy conjecture in the single-mode case. Specifically, we show that for any single-mode phase-covariant Gaussian channel Φ\Phi, the minimum of the von Neumann entropy S⁡(Φ⁡(ρ))S\big(\Phi(\rho)\big) over all single-mode states ρ\rho with a given lower bound on S⁡(ρ)S(\rho), is achieved at a thermal state.

1 Introduction

Quantum Gaussian channels are prototype noise models for the transmission of quantum information in current quantum communication technologies and information processing. In particular, they model transmission channels for sending quantum data encoded in bosonic systems through optical fibers and free space. Despite several developments in the past decades, there are still wide open conjectures regarding information theoretic properties of these channels. These conjectures are important not only due to the significance of quantum Gaussian channels in quantum information science, but also as quantum generalizations of some influential results in functional analysis.

In functional analysis and information theory, the optimality of Gaussian functions and Gaussian distributions has been established for various optimization problems involving Gaussian kernels or Gaussian channels. To name a few results, it is shown in [7] that only Gaussian functions saturate Gross’s celebrated logarithmic-Sobolev (log-Sobolev) inequality [25]. Also, it is shown in [36] that “Gaussian kernels have only Gaussian maximizers.” In information theory, it is shown that the optimal input distribution for Gaussian broadcast channels is Gaussian [20]. More generally, various inequalities including Brascamp-Lieb inequalities, the Loomis-Whitney inequality, the Prékopa-Leindler inequality, sharp form of Young’s inequality for convolution of functions as well as the entropy power inequality are tight for Gaussian functions and distributions; see [1] and references therein. Thus, it is tempting to verify the validity of these results in the non-commutative case for quantum Gaussian channels.

Single-mode quantum Gaussian channels have been classified in [30]; see also [31]. Among these classes are the three important physical classes of attenuator, amplifier and additive-noise channels, which have two main features. First, these channels are phase-covariant meaning, that they are covariant with respect to the group of phase operators, and second, they form quantum Markov semigroups [28]. These two features make these channels suitable candidates for generalizing some of the aforementioned properties of Gaussian kernels in functional analysis to the quantum case. In particular, as we show in this paper, these channels satisfy a new inequality that is saturated by Gaussian states, which we refer to as meta log-Sobolev inequality and provides a general framework for deriving quantum information-theoretic results regarding bosonic systems.

One application of our meta log-Sobolev inequality is to compute the optimal constants of the pp-log-Sobolev inequalities for a semigroup of attenuator channels, called the quantum (bosonic) Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup. This semigroup is of particular interest as it resembles its classical counterpart when acting on certain operators; see [9, Equation (7.5)]. The classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup is an important example of a Markov semigroup, which can be understood as the convolution of an input distribution by a Gaussian one. Its associated log-Sobolev inequality takes the form

12​Ent2​(f)≤‖f′‖22,∀f>0,\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\text{\rm Ent}_{2}(f)\leq\|f^{\prime}\|_{2}^{2},\qquad\quad\forall f>0, (1)

where the entropy Ent2​(f)=𝔼⁡[f2​log⁡f2]−𝔼⁡[f2]​log⁡𝔼⁡[f2]\text{\rm Ent}_{2}(f)=\mathbb{E}[f^{2}\log f^{2}]-\mathbb{E}[f^{2}]\log\mathbb{E}[f^{2}] and the 22-norm ‖f‖2=𝔼​[f2]1/2\|f\|_{2}=\mathbb{E}[f^{2}]^{1/2} are defined with respect to the standard normal distribution. This inequality was first established by Gross in his seminal work [25].

Given the log-Sobolev inequality (1) for the classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup and the development of the theory of hypercontractivity for quantum semigroups [39], it is natural to ask if the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup is hypercontractive and satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality.11 1 Amplifier and additive-noise channels are not hypercontractive in the usual sense. The 22-log-Sobolev inequality for the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup takes the form

α2​Ent2,σβ​(X)≤tr​(σβ​[𝐚,X]†​σβ​[𝐚,X]),∀X>0,tr​(σβ14​X​σβ14)2<+∞.\displaystyle\alpha_{2}\,\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\sigma_{\beta}}(X)\leq\text{\rm tr}\Big(\!\sqrt{\sigma_{\beta}}[\mathbf{a},X]^{\dagger}\sqrt{\sigma_{\beta}}[\mathbf{a},X]\Big),\qquad\forall X>0,\;\text{\rm tr}\Big(\sigma^{\frac{1}{4}}_{\beta}X\sigma_{\beta}^{\frac{1}{4}}\Big)^{2}\!\!<+\infty. (2)

Here, σβ=(1−e−β)​e−β​a†​a\sigma_{\beta}=(1-e^{-\beta})e^{-\beta a^{\dagger}a} is a thermal (and then Gaussian) state with parameter β>0\beta>0, [𝐚,X]=𝐚​X−X​𝐚[\mathbf{a},X]=\mathbf{a}X-X\mathbf{a} is the commutator of the annihilation operator with XX, and in the special case that ρ=(σβ14​X​σβ14)2\rho=\Big(\sigma^{\frac{1}{4}}_{\beta}X\sigma_{\beta}^{\frac{1}{4}}\Big)^{2} is a quantum state

Ent2,σβ(X)=D(ρ∥σβ)=tr(ρlogρ)−tr(ρlogσβ).\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\sigma_{\beta}}(X)=D(\rho\|\sigma_{\beta})=\text{\rm tr}(\rho\log\rho)-\text{\rm tr}(\rho\log\sigma_{\beta}).

Moreover, α2\alpha_{2} is called the 22-log-Sobolev constant whose optimal value, depending on β\beta, is one of our main problems of study in this work.

Using the spectral properties of the Lindbladian of the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup established in [9], a bound on the 2-log-Sobolev constant α2\alpha_{2} is derived in [6]. This bound confirms the hypercontractivity of the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup, yet it seems far from being optimal. Moreover, the bound of [6] works only in the single-mode case and is not clear to satisfy the so called tensorization property.

Although 22-log-Sobolev inequalities (assuming some regularity conditions [39, 35]) imply hypercontractivity inequalities, for a more refined characterization of the latter inequalities we need to establish generalizations of the above 22-log-Sobolev inequality for all values of 1≤p≤21\leq p\leq 2. These generalizations, called pp-log-Sobolev inequalities, are all equivalent and ignorant of the parameter pp for the classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup, yet they differ in the quantum case.22 2 The parameter pp is also relevant in the study of log-Sobolev inequalities for finite classical Markov semigroups; see [38] and references therein.

The 1-log-Sobolev (also called the modified log-Sobolev) inequality for the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup is first studied in [34] where it is examined for Gaussian states and it is conjectured that Gaussian states are optimal for the 11-log-Sobolev inequality. This conjecture is first proven in [8]. An alternative proof of this inequality and an extension are also derived in [12].

Our meta log-Sobolev inequality is also related to computing the classical capacity of attenuators, amplifiers and additive-noise channels, i.e., finding the maximum rate of reliable transmission of classical data through these channels. Since these channels are phase-covariant, their classical capacity is related to their minimum output entropy, i.e., the minimum entropy of their output states; see, e.g., [31]. It was a long-standing open problem that the minimum output entropy of these channels is additive and is achieved over Gaussian states [33, 21, 23]. This conjecture was answered in the affirmative in [22]. Extensions of this result have also been proven for which we refer to [32, 18] and references therein.

Generalizing the aforementioned minimum output entropy conjecture, the Constrained Minimum Output Entropy (CMOE) conjecture states that the minimum output entropy of the above phase-covariant Gaussian channels over input states with a given entropy is achieved by Gaussian states [27]. More precisely, the CMOE conjecture states that if Φ\Phi is a single-mode phase-covariant Gaussian channel, which by the above discussion is either attenuator, amplifier or additive-noise, then for any mm-mode state ρ\rho we have

1m​S​(Φ⊗m​(ρ))≥S⁡(Φ⁡(τ)),\displaystyle\frac{1}{m}S\big(\Phi^{\otimes m}(\rho)\big)\geq S(\Phi(\tau)), (3)

where τ\tau is a single-mode thermal state satisfying S⁡(τ)=1m​S​(ρ)S(\tau)=\frac{1}{m}S(\rho). This conjecture is in particular related to the problem of computing the capacity of quantum Gaussian broadcast channels [27]. Using tools developed in [14] the CMOE conjecture is proven in [15, 16] in the special case of m=1m=1. It is also proven for arbitrary mm in the parameter regime that the channel Φ\Phi becomes entanglement breaking [11].

Some other conjectures regarding the optimality of Gaussian states have also been proposed including an entropy photon-number inequality [26, 13] and a sharp Young’s inequality for the beam-splitter [18]. For more details on quantum Gaussian optimizer conjectures in quantum information theory we refer to [18].

1.1 Our contributions

In this paper, we introduce a meta log-Sobolev inequality for phase-covariant Gaussian quantum channels. In the Schrödinger picture, the Lindbladian of the semigroups of attenuator, amplifier and additive-noise channels mentioned above, takes the form

ℒ⁡(ρ)=ν0​(12​{𝐚𝐚†,ρ}−𝐚†​ρ​𝐚)+ν1​(12​{𝐚†​𝐚,ρ}−𝐚​ρ​𝐚†),\mathcal{L}(\rho)=\nu_{0}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},\rho\}-\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\rho\mathbf{a}\Big)+\nu_{1}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\{\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a},\rho\}-\mathbf{a}\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\Big),

where ν0,ν1≥0\nu_{0},\nu_{1}\geq 0 are non-negative constants and {X,Y}=X​Y+Y​X\{X,Y\}=XY+YX denotes anti-commutator. Then, given any ω≥0\omega\geq 0, we define the function

Υ⁡(ρ)=pp−1​tr​(ℒ⁡(ρ1/p)​ρ1−1/p)+ω​tr​(ρ​𝐚†​𝐚)+S⁡(ρ),\displaystyle\Upsilon(\rho)=\frac{p}{p-1}\text{\rm tr}\Big(\mathcal{L}\big(\rho^{1/p}\big)\rho^{1-1/p}\Big)+\omega\,\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}\big)+S(\rho),

over single-mode states ρ\rho. Later, we will see that for the choice of

X=σβ−12​p​ρ1p​σβ−12​p,X=\sigma_{\beta}^{-\frac{1}{2p}}\rho^{\frac{1}{p}}\sigma_{\beta}^{-\frac{1}{2p}},

and p=2p=2, the first term in Υ⁡(ρ)\Upsilon(\rho) resembles the Dirichlet form appearing on the right hand side of (2). In this case, Entp,σβ(X)=D(ρ∥σβ)\text{\rm Ent}_{p,\sigma_{\beta}}(X)=D(\rho\|\sigma_{\beta}) can be written in terms of the other two terms in Υ⁡(ρ)\Upsilon(\rho). Thus, computing the infimum of Υ⁡(ρ)\Upsilon(\rho) is useful in obtaining the optimal log-Sobolev constant αp\alpha_{p}.

Our main result, which we call a meta log-Sobolev inequality, states that optimal states in the minimization of Υ⁡(ρ)\Upsilon(\rho) are thermal, i.e.,

Υ(ρ)≥infτ: thermalΥ(τ),\displaystyle\Upsilon(\rho)\geq\inf_{\tau:\text{ \rm thermal}}\Upsilon\big(\tau\big), (4)

for any state ρ\rho of a single-mode bosonic system.

By using (4), we turn the problem of computing the optimal pp-log-Sobolev constant αp\alpha_{p} into an optimization problem over thermal states that are characterized by a single real parameter. We explicitly compute the optimal constant for the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup for any 1≤p≤21\leq p\leq 2:

αp=p​p^4​βeβ/2(1−e−β/p)(1−e−β/p^).\displaystyle\alpha_{p}=\frac{p\hat{p}}{4\beta}e^{\beta/2}\big(1-e^{-\beta/p}\big)\big(1-e^{-\beta/\hat{p}}\big). (5)

This result for p=1p=1 recovers the modified log-Sobolev inequality of [8], and for p=2p=2 is an improvement over the bound of [6].

We also study the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup in the multimode case. It is well-known that log-Sobolev constants for classical Markov semigroups have the tensorization property (see, e.g., [38]), meaning that considering the mm-fold tensor product of the semigroup, the log-Sobolev constants of the resulting semigroup are the same as those of the original one. This property is not known to hold for arbitrary quantum Markov semigroups. Thus, we also consider the mm-mode version of (2):

α^2​Ent2,σβ⊗m​(X)≤∑j=1mtr​(σβ⊗m​[𝐚j,X]†​σβ⊗m​[𝐚j,X]),\widehat{\alpha}_{2}\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\sigma_{\beta}^{\otimes m}}(X)\leq\sum_{j=1}^{m}\text{\rm tr}\Big(\!\sqrt{\sigma_{\beta}^{\otimes m}}[\mathbf{a}_{j},X]^{\dagger}\sqrt{\sigma_{\beta}^{\otimes m}}[\mathbf{a}_{j},X]\Big),

where X>0X>0 runs over mm-mode operators, and α^2\widehat{\alpha}_{2} is the 22-log-Sobolev constant for the mm-fold tensor product semigroup. We show that for any m>1m>1,

α^2≥(2+log⁡(2​m+1)sinh⁡(β/2)+1α2)−1,\displaystyle\widehat{\alpha}_{2}\geq\bigg(\frac{2+\log(2m+1)}{\sinh(\beta/2)}+\frac{1}{\alpha_{2}}\bigg)^{-1}\!, (6)

where α2\alpha_{2} is given by (5).

To prove our result (6), we follow the approach of [6]. We use properties of the spectrum of the generator ℒ\mathcal{L} of the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup to reduce the problem for arbitrary mm-mode operators XX to operators that are diagonal in the number basis. To this end, we prove an entropic inequality which might be of independent interest. Next, restricting to diagonal operators, we obtain an essentially classical Markov semigroup that is known to satisfy the tensorization property. Thus, the problem for mm-mode states is reduced to that of single-mode states for which we have already established the optimal log-Sobolev constant in (5). We note that, although, our first step of the proof is inspired by [6], our penalty term that compensates for the reduction to diagonal states is smaller than that of [6]. Moreover, as mentioned above we compute the exact value of the 22-log-Sobolev constant for diagonal states while [6] derives only a lower bound. Thus, our estimate on the 22-log-Sobolev inequality is not just an mm-mode generalization of [6], but a twofold improvement thereof.

Our meta log-Sobolev inequality (4) provides a general framework that can be applied in other settings as well. In this paper, using (4) we also give an alternative proof of the CMOE conjecture (3) in the case of m=1m=1.

Outline of the paper:

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review the class of single-mode phase-covariant Gaussian channels. We argue that these channels form semigroups and compute their Lindbladians. Section 3 is devoted to our meta log-Sobolev inequality (4) and its proof. The log-Sobolev constants for the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup are computed in Section 4. Also, our proof of the CMOE conjecture is given in Section 5. Final remarks are discussed in Section 6 and some detailed computations are left for the appendices.

2 Phase-covariance Gaussian channels

A single-mode bosonic continuous-variable system is described by the annihilation operator 𝐚\mathbf{a} and it hermitian conjugate, the creation operator 𝐚†\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}. These operators satisfy the bosonic commutation relation

[𝐚,𝐚†]=𝐚𝐚†−𝐚†​𝐚=1.[\mathbf{a},\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}]=\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}-\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}=1.

Fock states {|n⟩:n≥0}\{|n\rangle:\,n\geq 0\}, also called number states, form an orthonormal basis for the corresponding Hilbert space and are eigenvectors of 𝐚†​𝐚\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a} called the number operator: 𝐚†​𝐚​|n⟩=n​|n⟩\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}|n\rangle=n|n\rangle. We indeed have 𝐚​|n⟩=n​|n−1⟩\mathbf{a}|n\rangle=\sqrt{n}|n-1\rangle and 𝐚†​|n⟩=n+1​|n+1⟩\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}|n\rangle=\sqrt{n+1}|n+1\rangle. Single-mode quantum states ρ\rho are density operators (ρ⪰0\rho\succeq 0 and tr​(ρ)=1\text{\rm tr}(\rho)=1) acting on this Hilbert space.

All states that we consider in this paper are assumed to be physical and hence have finite mean photon number. More precisely, for a pure state ρ=|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|\rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi| we assume that |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle belongs to the domain of 𝐚\mathbf{a} and ⟨ψ|𝐚†​𝐚|ψ⟩=‖𝐚⁡|ψ⟩‖2<+∞\langle\psi|\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}|\psi\rangle=\|\mathbf{a}|\psi\rangle\|^{2}<+\infty, and more generally for a mixed state with eigen-decomposition ρ=∑j=0∞λj​|ψj⟩​⟨ψj|\rho=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\lambda_{j}|\psi_{j}\rangle\langle\psi_{j}| we assume that |ψj⟩|\psi_{j}\rangle, for any jj with λj>0\lambda_{j}>0, belongs to the domain of 𝐚\mathbf{a} and ∑jλj​‖𝐚⁡|ψj⟩‖2<+∞\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}\|\mathbf{a}|\psi_{j}\rangle\|^{2}<+\infty. The latter expression is indeed equal to tr​(𝐚​ρ​𝐚†)\text{\rm tr}(\mathbf{a}\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}), yet we often write it as tr​(ρ​𝐚†​𝐚)\text{\rm tr}(\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}), the conventional notation for the mean photon number, considering the following formal definition for the expectation value of an operator in quantum mechanics.33 3 Note that although tr​(𝐚​ρ​𝐚†)\text{\rm tr}(\mathbf{a}\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}) may be well-defined and finite, ρ​𝐚†​𝐚\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a} may not be a trace class operator. For more details on the expectation value of unbounded operators in quantum mechanics we refer to [4]. For any positive semidefinite operator XX, we formally define tr​(ρ​X)=∑jλj​‖X1/2​|ψj⟩‖2\text{\rm tr}(\rho X)=\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}\|X^{1/2}|\psi_{j}\rangle\|^{2} if |ψj⟩|\psi_{j}\rangle belongs to the domain of X1/2X^{1/2} for all jj with λj>0\lambda_{j}>0, and let tr​(ρ​X)=+∞\text{\rm tr}(\rho X)=+\infty otherwise.44 4 Note that ‖𝐚⁡|ψ⟩‖=‖|𝐚†​𝐚|1/2​|ψ⟩‖\|\mathbf{a}|\psi\rangle\|=\||\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}|^{1/2}|\psi\rangle\|, so this definition matches the one for the number operator. Also, for a self-adjoint operator XX with decomposition X=X+−X−X=X_{+}-X_{-} where both X+,X−X_{+},X_{-} are positive semidefinite, we define tr​(ρ​X)=tr​(ρ​X+)−tr​(ρ​X−)\text{\rm tr}(\rho X)=\text{\rm tr}(\rho X_{+})-\text{\rm tr}(\rho X_{-}).

Quantum states can be represented in terms of displacement (Weyl) operators Dξ=exp⁡(ξ​𝐚†−ξ¯​𝐚)D_{\xi}=\exp(\xi\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}-\bar{\xi}\mathbf{a}) with ξ∈ℂ\xi\in\mathbb{C} as

ρ=1π​∫ℂχρ​(ξ)​D−ξ​d2​ξ,\rho=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\chi_{\rho}(\xi)D_{-\xi}\,\text{\rm{d}}^{2}\xi, (7)

where χρ​(ξ)=tr​(ρ​Dξ)\chi_{\rho}(\xi)=\text{\rm tr}(\rho D_{\xi}) is called the characteristic function [5]. The characteristic function is the Fourier transform of the Wigner function [29].

A quantum state is called Gaussian if its characteristic and equivalently Wigner functions are Gaussian. Therefore, Gaussian states can be simply described in terms of the first-order and second-order moments of their Wigner function. Thermal states are an important class of Gaussian states. A thermal state with parameter β>0\beta>0 that is proportional to the inverse of temperature, is diagonal in the Fock basis and is given by

σβ=1tr​(e−β​𝐚†​𝐚)​e−β​𝐚†​𝐚=(1−e−β)​∑n=0∞e−n​β​|n⟩​⟨n|.\sigma_{\beta}=\frac{1}{\text{\rm tr}(e^{-\beta\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}})}e^{-\beta\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}}=(1-e^{-\beta})\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}e^{-n\beta}|n\rangle\langle n|. (8)

The characteristic function of this thermal state equals

χσβ​(ξ)=e−12​coth⁡(β/2)​|ξ|2.\displaystyle\chi_{\sigma_{\beta}}(\xi)=e^{-\frac{1}{2}\coth(\beta/2)|\xi|^{2}}. (9)

At zero temperature (β=∞\beta=\infty) we obtain the vacuum state σ∞=|0⟩​⟨0|\sigma_{\infty}=|0\rangle\langle 0|.

The evolution of quantum systems, in general, is described by quantum channels Φ\Phi that are linear completely positive and trace-preserving superoperators. Quantum channels that transform Gaussian states into Gaussian states are known as Gaussian channels [33, 3, 42, 31]. Gaussian channels that are unitary are called Gaussian unitaries.

A single-mode Gaussian channels is called phase-covariant55 5 Phase-covariant channels are also known as gauge-covariant channels. [22, 24] if it satisfies

Φ⁡(Uθ​ρ​Uθ†)=Uθ​Φ​(ρ)​Uθ†,\Phi\big(U_{\theta}\rho\,U_{\theta}^{\dagger}\big)=U_{\theta}\Phi(\rho)U_{\theta}^{\dagger}, (10)

for any state ρ\rho and θ∈[0,2​π)\theta\in[0,2\pi), where Uθ=ei​θ​𝐚†​𝐚U_{\theta}=e^{i\theta\,\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}} is the phase-rotation unitary. By the classification of single-mode Gaussian channels [31, 30], a single-mode phase-covariant Gaussian channel can be described in terms of its action on the characteristic function. For any such channel there are parameters γ,λ≥0\gamma,\lambda\geq 0 such that

χΦ⁡(ρ)​(ξ)=e−12​γ​|ξ|2​χρ​(λ​ξ),\chi_{\Phi(\rho)}(\xi)=e^{-\frac{1}{2}\gamma|\xi|^{2}}\chi_{\rho}\big(\!\sqrt{\lambda}\xi\big), (11)

where the complete positivity condition implies γ≥|1−λ|\gamma\geq|1-\lambda| [33]. The channel Φ\Phi is called quantum limited if γ=|1−λ|\gamma=|1-\lambda|. By using the characteristic function of thermal states (9) in (11), one can verify that phase-covariant Gaussian channels transform thermal states to thermal states.

Single-mode phase-covariant Gaussian channels consist of three classes of attenuator channels corresponding to 0≤λ<10\leq\lambda<1, additive-noise channels corresponding to λ=1\lambda=1, and amplifier channels corresponding 1<λ1<\lambda. These are important physical channels in describing dynamics of continuous-variable quantum systems.

A crucial property of single-mode phase-covariant Gaussian channels is that they admit semigroup structures [28, 23]. Specifically, any such channel can be written as Φt0=e−t0​ℒ\Phi_{t_{0}}=e^{-t_{0}\mathcal{L}} for some t0≥0t_{0}\geq 0 where {Φt=e−t​ℒ:t≥0}\big\{\Phi_{t}=e^{-t\mathcal{L}}:\,t\geq 0\big\} is a semigroup of single-mode phase-covariant Gaussian channels. We show in Appendix A that the corresponding Lindbladian ℒ\mathcal{L} of such a semigroup takes the form

ℒ⁡(ρ)=ν0​(12​{𝐚𝐚†,ρ}−𝐚†​ρ​𝐚)+ν1​(12​{𝐚†​𝐚,ρ}−𝐚​ρ​𝐚†),\mathcal{L}(\rho)=\nu_{0}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},\rho\}-\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\rho\,\mathbf{a}\Big)+\nu_{1}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\{\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a},\rho\}-\mathbf{a}\,\rho\,\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\Big), (12)

where {X,Y}=X​Y+Y​X\{X,Y\}=XY+YX denotes the anti-commutator, and ν0,ν1≥0\nu_{0},\nu_{1}\geq 0 are parameters determining the semigroup. We argue in Appendix A that three ranges for the parameters ν0,ν1\nu_{0},\nu_{1} give the three classes of single-mode phase-covariant channels: ν1>ν0\nu_{1}>\nu_{0} corresponds to attenuator channels, ν0=ν1\nu_{0}=\nu_{1} corresponds to additive-noise channels, and ν1<ν0\nu_{1}<\nu_{0} corresponds to amplifier channels.

Attenuator channels, in general, can be physically modeled by applying a beam splitter unitary with the transmissivity of 0≤λ≤10\leq\lambda\leq 1 on the system and an auxiliary system in the thermal state σβ\sigma_{\beta}, and then tracing out the second subsystem:

Φλatt​(ρ)=tr2​(UBS,λ​(ρ⊗σβ)​UBS,λ†).\Phi^{\text{att}}_{\lambda}(\rho)=\text{\rm tr}_{2}\Big(U_{\text{BS},\lambda}(\rho\otimes\sigma_{\beta})U_{\text{BS},\lambda}^{\dagger}\Big). (13)

The characteristic function of the output state is given by

χΦλatt​(ρ)​(ξ)=e−12​coth⁡(β/2)​(1−λ)​|ξ|2​χρ​(λ​ξ).\chi_{\Phi^{\text{att}}_{\lambda}(\rho)}(\xi)=e^{-\frac{1}{2}\coth(\beta/2)(1-\lambda)|\xi|^{2}}\chi_{\rho}(\sqrt{\lambda}\xi).

Choosing the transmissivity parameter λt=e−2​c​t\lambda_{t}=e^{-2ct} as a function of time, where c>0c>0 is some constant, we obtain a semigroup of attenuation channels. The generator of this semigroup given in (12) has parameters ν0=c⁡(coth⁡(β/2)−1)\nu_{0}=c\left(\coth(\beta/2)-1\right) and ν1=c⁡(coth⁡(β/2)+1)\nu_{1}=c\left(\coth(\beta/2)+1\right). Note that for the special choice of c=sinh⁡(β/2)c=\sinh(\beta/2) we have ν0=e−β/2\nu_{0}=e^{-\beta/2} and ν1=eβ/2\nu_{1}=e^{\beta/2}. This semigroup of attenuator channels is sometimes called the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup.

Amplifier channels can be described by replacing the beam splitter unitary in the above model by a two-mode squeezing unitary to get

Φλamp​(ρ)=tr2​(U2S,λ​(ρ⊗σβ)​U2S,λ†),\Phi^{\text{amp}}_{\lambda}(\rho)=\text{\rm tr}_{2}\Big(U_{\text{2S},\lambda}(\rho\otimes\sigma_{\beta})U_{\text{2S},\lambda}^{\dagger}\Big), (14)

where λ≥1\lambda\geq 1 is the squeezing parameter. In this case, the relation between input and output characteristic functions becomes

χΦλatt​(ρ)​(ξ)=e−12​coth⁡(β/2)​(λ−1)​|ξ|2​χρ​(λ​ξ).\chi_{\Phi^{\text{att}}_{\lambda}(\rho)}(\xi)=e^{-\frac{1}{2}\coth(\beta/2)(\lambda-1)|\xi|^{2}}\chi_{\rho}(\sqrt{\lambda}\xi).

Choosing λt=e2​c​t\lambda_{t}=e^{2ct} with c>0c>0 to be a function of time, we obtain a semigroup with the generator corresponding to parameters ν0=c⁡(coth⁡(β/2)+1)\nu_{0}=c\left(\coth(\beta/2)+1\right) and ν1=c⁡(coth⁡(β/2)−1)\nu_{1}=c\left(\coth(\beta/2)-1\right) in (12).

Additive-noise channels can be modeled by applying a displacement operator whose parameter is chosen at random according to a Gaussian probability distribution:

Φγadd​(ρ)=2π​γ​∫e−2γ​|ξ|2​Dξ​ρ​Dξ†​d2​ξ.\Phi^{\text{add}}_{\gamma}(\rho)=\frac{2}{\pi\gamma}\int e^{-\frac{2}{\gamma}|\xi|^{2}}D_{\xi}\rho D^{\dagger}_{\xi}\,\text{\rm{d}}^{2}\xi.

This channel in terms of characteristic functions can be written as

χΦγadd​(ρ)​(ξ)=e−12​γ​|ξ|2​χρ​(ξ).\chi_{\Phi^{\text{add}}_{\gamma}(\rho)}(\xi)=e^{-\frac{1}{2}\gamma|\xi|^{2}}\chi_{\rho}(\xi).

Again, by setting γt=2​c​t\gamma_{t}=2ct with c>0c>0 we obtain a semigroup whose generator given by (12) has parameters ν0=ν1=c\nu_{0}=\nu_{1}=c. This semigroup is sometimes called the quantum heat semigroup.

We emphasize that by the above discussion any single-mode phase-covariant channel (11) can be viewed as a member of one of the above three semigroups. The point is that, the above choices of parameters λt,γt\lambda_{t},\gamma_{t} cover all the valid ranges of λ,γ\lambda,\gamma in (11).

In this paper, we also consider mm-mode bosonic systems, described by mm pairs of annihilation and creation operators {𝐚1,𝐚1†,…,𝐚m,𝐚m†}\{\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{1}^{\dagger},\dots,\mathbf{a}_{m},\mathbf{a}_{m}^{\dagger}\} satisfying [𝐚i,𝐚j]=0[\mathbf{a}_{i},\mathbf{a}_{j}]=0 and [𝐚i,𝐚j†]=δi,j[\mathbf{a}_{i},\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}]=\delta_{i,j}. Vectors of the associated tensor product Hilbert space can be expressed in terms of mm-mode number states {|n1,…,nm⟩:n1,…,nm≥0}\{|n_{1},\dots,n_{m}\rangle:\,n_{1},\dots,n_{m}\geq 0\}. Also, the characteristic function for an mm-mode state ρ\rho is given by χρ​(ξ)=tr​(ρ​Dξ)\chi_{\rho}(\xi)=\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho D_{\xi}\big), where ξ=(ξ1,…,ξm)∈ℂm\xi=(\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{m})\in\mathbb{C}^{m} and Dξ=Dξ1⊗⋯⊗DξmD_{\xi}=D_{\xi_{1}}\otimes\dots\otimes D_{\xi_{m}}. As in the single-mode case, physical multimode states ρ\rho considered in this paper have finite mean photon number: tr​(ρ​Hm)<+∞\text{\rm tr}(\rho H_{m})<+\infty, where Hm=∑j=1m𝐚j†​𝐚jH_{m}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j} is the mm-mode number operator. The definitions of Gaussian channels and unitaries can be extended to the multimode case. Any Gaussian unitary can be decomposed into displacement operators, mutlimode passive transformations, which preserve the mean photon number, and single-mode squeezing transformations; see [41] for more details.

3 Meta log-Sobolev inequality

As discussed in the previous section, all the Lindbladians associated to single-mode phase-covariant channels have the form ℒ=ν0​ℒ0+ν1​ℒ1\mathcal{L}=\nu_{0}\mathcal{L}_{0}+\nu_{1}\mathcal{L}_{1} for some ν0,ν1≥0\nu_{0},\nu_{1}\geq 0 where

ℒ0​(X)=12​{𝐚𝐚†,X}−𝐚†​X​𝐚,ℒ1​(X)=12​{𝐚†​𝐚,X}−𝐚​X​𝐚†.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{0}(X)=\frac{1}{2}\{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},X\}-\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}X\mathbf{a},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{1}(X)=\frac{1}{2}\{\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a},X\}-\mathbf{a}X\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}. (15)

Let ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle denote the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product:

⟨X,Y⟩=tr​(X†​Y).\langle X,Y\rangle=\text{\rm tr}(X^{\dagger}Y).

Also, let ℒ∗\mathcal{L}^{*} be the adjoint of the generator ℒ\mathcal{L} with respect to this inner product: ⟨X,ℒ⁡(Y)⟩=⟨ℒ∗​(X),Y⟩\langle X,\mathcal{L}(Y)\rangle=\langle\mathcal{L}^{*}(X),Y\rangle. Indeed, ℒ∗\mathcal{L}^{*} is the generator in the Heisenberg picture given by

ℒ∗​(X)=ν0​(12​{𝐚𝐚†,X}−𝐚​X​𝐚†)+ν1​(12​{𝐚†​𝐚,X}−𝐚†​X​𝐚).\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{*}(X)=\nu_{0}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},X\}-\mathbf{a}X\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\Big)+\nu_{1}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\{\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a},X\}-\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}X\mathbf{a}\Big).

Let p≥1p\geq 1 and p^\hat{p} be the Hölder conjugate of pp given by66 6 If p=1p=1, we let p^=+∞\hat{p}=+\infty.

1p+1p^=1.\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{\hat{p}}=1.

Then, for any single-mode quantum state ρ\rho define

Υ⁡(ρ)\displaystyle\Upsilon(\rho) :=p^​⟨ℒ⁡(ρ1/p),ρ1/p^⟩+ω​tr​(ρ​𝐚†​𝐚)+S⁡(ρ)\displaystyle:=\hat{p}\big\langle\mathcal{L}\big(\rho^{1/p}\big),\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle+\omega\text{\rm tr}(\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a})+S(\rho)
=p^​(ν0​⟨ℒ0​(ρ1/p),ρ1/p^⟩+ν1​⟨ℒ1​(ρ1/p),ρ1/p^⟩)+ω​tr​(ρ​𝐚†​𝐚)+S⁡(ρ),\displaystyle\,=\hat{p}\Big(\!\nu_{0}\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{0}\big(\rho^{1/p}\big),\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle+\nu_{1}\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{1}\big(\rho^{1/p}\big),\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle\!\Big)+\omega\text{\rm tr}(\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a})+S(\rho), (16)

where ω≥0\omega\geq 0 is a fixed parameter and S​(ρ)=−tr​(ρ​log⁡ρ)S(\rho)=-\text{\rm tr}(\rho\log\rho) is the von Neumann entropy of the state. The factor p^\hat{p} in the first term of Υ⁡(ρ)\Upsilon(\rho) is for the sake of normalization in the limiting case of p→1+p\to 1^{+}. Indeed, since ℒ∗​(I)=0\mathcal{L}^{*}(I)=0, we have

limp→1+p^​⟨ℒ⁡(ρ1/p),ρ1/p^⟩=limp→1+p^​⟨ρ1/p,ℒ∗​(ρ1/p^)⟩=⟨ρ,ℒ∗​(log⁡ρ)⟩=⟨ℒ⁡(ρ),log⁡ρ⟩.\lim_{p\to 1^{+}}\hat{p}\big\langle\mathcal{L}\big(\rho^{1/p}\big),\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle=\lim_{p\to 1^{+}}\hat{p}\,\big\langle\rho^{1/p},\mathcal{L}^{*}\big(\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\big)\big\rangle=\langle\rho,\mathcal{L}^{*}(\log\rho)\rangle=\langle\mathcal{L}(\rho),\log\rho\rangle.

Thus, by convention for p=1p=1 we let p^​⟨ℒ⁡(ρ1/p),ρ1/p^⟩=⟨ℒ⁡(ρ),log⁡ρ⟩\hat{p}\,\big\langle\mathcal{L}\big(\rho^{1/p}\big),\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle=\langle\mathcal{L}(\rho),\log\rho\rangle.

A straightforward computation verifies that

Υ⁡(ρ)=p^​(ν0​[tr​(ρ​𝐚𝐚†)−tr​(ρ1/p​𝐚​ρ1/p^​𝐚†)]+ν1​[tr​(ρ​𝐚†​𝐚)−tr​(ρ1/p​𝐚†​ρ1/p^​𝐚)])+ω​tr​(ρ​𝐚†​𝐚)+S⁡(ρ).\displaystyle\Upsilon(\rho)=\hat{p}\bigg(\!\nu_{0}\Big[\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)-\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho^{1/p}\mathbf{a}\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)\Big]+\nu_{1}\Big[\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}\big)-\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho^{1/p}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\mathbf{a}\big)\!\Big]\!\bigg)+\omega\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}\big)+S(\rho). (17)

We may think of this equation as the starting definition of Υ⁡(ρ)\Upsilon(\rho). In Appendix B, we show that if ρ\rho has a finite mean photon number, then all the terms in the above equation are finite and Υ⁡(ρ)\Upsilon(\rho) given by (17) is well-defined.

One of the main technical contributions of our work is that the infimum of Υ⁡(ρ)\Upsilon(\rho) over states ρ\rho is achieved at single-mode thermal states. To this end, it would be beneficial to compute Υ⁡(ρ)\Upsilon(\rho) for thermal states. Using (17), for a single-mode thermal state,77 7 Hereafter, we use τ\tau to denote a thermal state on which we optimize, and save σ=σβ\sigma=\sigma_{\beta} for the reference thermal state in our description of phase-covariant Gaussian channels; see equations (13) and (14).

τ=τx=(1−x)​∑nxn​|n⟩​⟨n|,\tau=\tau_{x}=(1-x)\sum_{n}x^{n}|n\rangle\langle n|,

where we put 0<x=e−β<10<x=e^{-\beta}<1 in (8), we have

Υ⁡(τ)\displaystyle\Upsilon(\tau) =p^(1−x)∑n(ν0(1−x1/p^)(n+1)xn+ν1(1−x−1/p^)nxn)\displaystyle=\hat{p}(1-x)\sum_{n}\Big(\nu_{0}(1-x^{1/\hat{p}})(n+1)x^{n}+\nu_{1}(1-x^{-1/\hat{p}})nx^{n}\Big)
+ω(1−x)∑nnxn−(1−x)∑nxnlog((1−x)xn)\displaystyle\quad~+\omega(1-x)\sum_{n}nx^{n}-(1-x)\sum_{n}x^{n}\log\big((1-x)x^{n}\big)
=p^(1−x)(ν0(1−x1/p^)1(1−x)2+ν1(1−x−1/p^)x(1−x)2)\displaystyle=\hat{p}(1-x)\Big(\nu_{0}(1-x^{1/\hat{p}})\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}+\nu_{1}(1-x^{-1/\hat{p}})\frac{x}{(1-x)^{2}}\Big)
+ω⁡(1−x)​x(1−x)2−(1−x)​x(1−x)2​log⁡x−log⁡(1−x)\displaystyle\quad~+\omega(1-x)\frac{x}{(1-x)^{2}}-(1-x)\frac{x}{(1-x)^{2}}\log x-\log(1-x)
=p^1−x​(ν0​(1−x1/p^)+ν1​(x−x1/p))+ω​x1−x−x1−x​log⁡x−log⁡(1−x).\displaystyle=\frac{\hat{p}}{1-x}\Big(\nu_{0}(1-x^{1/\hat{p}})+\nu_{1}(x-x^{1/p})\Big)+\omega\frac{x}{1-x}-\frac{x}{1-x}\log x-\log(1-x). (18)

Optimizing over the choice of the thermal state τ\tau, we define

ηth\displaystyle\eta_{\text{\rm{th}}} :=infτ: thermalΥ(τ)\displaystyle:=\inf_{\tau:\text{ \rm thermal}}\Upsilon(\tau)
=inf0<x<1p^1−x​(ν0​(1−x1/p^)+ν1​(x−x1/p))+ω​x1−x−x1−x​log⁡x−log⁡(1−x).\displaystyle\,=\inf_{0<x<1}\,\frac{\hat{p}}{1-x}\Big(\nu_{0}(1-x^{1/\hat{p}})+\nu_{1}(x-x^{1/p})\Big)+\omega\frac{x}{1-x}-\frac{x}{1-x}\log x-\log(1-x). (19)
Theorem 1.

[Meta log-Sobolev inequality] For any ν0,ν1,ω≥0\nu_{0},\nu_{1},\omega\geq 0 and p≥1p\geq 1 define Υ⁡(ρ)\Upsilon(\rho) by (16). Let ηth\eta_{\text{\rm{th}}} be the infimum of Υ⁡(τ)\Upsilon(\tau) over thermal states as in (19). Then, for any single-mode quantum state ρ\rho with finite mean photon number we have

Υ⁡(ρ)≥ηth.\displaystyle\Upsilon(\rho)\geq\eta_{\text{\rm{th}}}. (20)

The proof of this theorem is broken into two steps:

  • (i)

    The first step is to reduce the problem for arbitrary states ρ\rho to states that are diagonal in the Fock basis. To this end, we use ideas developed in [14]. We show that, fixing the eigenvalues of ρ\rho and rotating its eigen-basis, we can obtain a diagonal state ρ^\widehat{\rho} that satisfies Υ⁡(ρ)≥Υ⁡(ρ^)\Upsilon(\rho)\geq\Upsilon(\widehat{\rho}). We then conclude that diagonal states are sufficient when minimizing Υ⁡(⋅)\Upsilon(\cdot).

  • (ii)

    In the second step, we show that the optimal diagonal states are thermal. The proof idea in this step is extracted from tensorization type arguments. Tensorization was first used by Gross [25] for proving his celebrated log-Sobolev inequality. The idea in [25] is that by the central limit theorem, an expectation value with respect to a Gaussian distribution can be understood as the limit n→+∞n\to+\infty of the expectation value of some lifted function on the product space {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n} with respect to a product probability measure. Here, being interested in thermal states, our distributions of reference are geometric distributions, and geometric distributions can be understood in terms of the first success in a sequence of independent Bernoulli trials. Thus, it is natural to employ a tensorization type argument in order to reduce the optimization over general single-mode diagonal states to thermal ones. In our proof, we do not directly refer to Bernoulli trials, yet our intuition on why and how it works is really rooted in a tensorization argument as described here.

Proof.

(i) In the first step of the proof we show that for any state ρ\rho, there is a state ρ^\widehat{\rho} that is diagonal in the Fock basis and satisfies Υ⁡(ρ)≥Υ⁡(ρ^)\Upsilon(\rho)\geq\Upsilon(\widehat{\rho}).

Let

ρ=∑n=0∞λn​|ψn⟩​⟨ψn|,\rho=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\lambda_{n}|\psi_{n}\rangle\langle\psi_{n}|,

be the eigen-decomposition of ρ\rho where λ0≥λ1≥⋯≥0\lambda_{0}\geq\lambda_{1}\geq\cdots\geq 0 are the eigenvalues of ρ\rho and {|ψn⟩:n≥0}\{|\psi_{n}\rangle:\,n\geq 0\} is its eigen-basis. In this case, there are rk=λk−λk+1≥0r_{k}=\lambda_{k}-\lambda_{k+1}\geq 0 such that

ρ=∑k=0∞rk​Pk,\rho=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}r_{k}P_{k},

where Pk=∑n=0k|ψn⟩​⟨ψn|P_{k}=\sum_{n=0}^{k}|\psi_{n}\rangle\langle\psi_{n}| is the projection operator on the first k+1k+1 eigenvectors of ρ\rho. Now we define

ρ^=∑k=0∞rk​Πk,\widehat{\rho}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}r_{k}\Pi_{k},

where Πk=∑n=0k|n⟩​⟨n|\Pi_{k}=\sum_{n=0}^{k}|n\rangle\langle n| is the projection operator on the first k+1k+1 vectors in the Fock basis. We note that by definition, ρ^=∑k=0nλk​|n⟩​⟨n|\widehat{\rho}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\lambda_{k}|n\rangle\langle n| is diagonal in the Fock basis and shares the same eigenvalues with ρ\rho. Therefore, they have the same entropy

S⁡(ρ^)=S⁡(ρ).\displaystyle S(\widehat{\rho})=S(\rho). (21)

Next, we note that the infimum of tr​(Qk​𝐚†​𝐚)\text{\rm tr}(Q_{k}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}) over projectors QkQ_{k} with rank k+1k+1, equals the sum of the first k+1k+1 smallest eigenvalues of 𝐚†​𝐚\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}, and is achieved by Qk=ΠkQ_{k}=\Pi_{k}. This implies that the mean photon number of ρ\rho is lower bounded by that of ρ^\widehat{\rho}:

tr​(ρ​𝐚†​𝐚)\displaystyle\text{\rm tr}(\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}) =∑krk​tr​(Pk​𝐚†​𝐚)≥∑krk​tr​(Πk​𝐚†​𝐚)=tr​(ρ^​𝐚†​𝐚).\displaystyle=\sum_{k}r_{k}\text{\rm tr}(P_{k}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a})\geq\sum_{k}r_{k}\text{\rm tr}(\Pi_{k}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a})=\text{\rm tr}(\widehat{\rho}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}). (22)

We also have

⟨ℒ0​(ρ1/p),ρ1/p^⟩=tr​(ρ​𝐚𝐚†)−tr​(ρ1/p​𝐚​ρ1/p^​𝐚†)=tr​(ρ1/p​ρ1/p^​𝐚𝐚†)−tr​(ρ1/p​𝐚​ρ1/p^​𝐚†).\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{0}\big(\rho^{1/p}\big),\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle=\text{\rm tr}(\rho\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger})-\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho^{1/p}\mathbf{a}\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)=\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho^{1/p}\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)-\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho^{1/p}\mathbf{a}\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big).

We note that ρ1/p=∑nλn1/p​|ψn⟩​⟨ψn|\rho^{1/p}=\sum_{n}\lambda_{n}^{1/p}|\psi_{n}\rangle\langle\psi_{n}| with λ01/p≥λ11/p≥⋯≥0\lambda_{0}^{1/p}\geq\lambda_{1}^{1/p}\geq\cdots\geq 0. Then, there are rp,k≥0r_{p,k}\geq 0 such that ρ1/p=∑krp,k​Pk\rho^{1/p}=\sum_{k}r_{p,k}P_{k}. Similarly, there are rp^,k≥0r_{\hat{p},k}\geq 0 such that ρ1/p^=∑krp^,k​Pk\rho^{1/\hat{p}}=\sum_{k}r_{\hat{p},k}P_{k}. We also have ρ^1/p=∑krp,k​Πk\widehat{\rho}^{1/p}=\sum_{k}r_{p,k}\Pi_{k} and ρ^1/p^=∑krp^,k​Πk\widehat{\rho}^{1/\hat{p}}=\sum_{k}r_{\hat{p},k}\Pi_{k}. Therefore, we have

⟨ℒ0\displaystyle\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{0} (ρ1/p),ρ1/p^⟩=∑k,ℓrp,krp^,ℓ(tr(PkPℓ𝐚𝐚†)−tr(Pk𝐚Pℓ𝐚†))\displaystyle\big(\rho^{1/p}\big),\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle=\sum_{k,\ell}r_{p,k}\,r_{\hat{p},\ell}\Big(\!\text{\rm tr}\big(P_{k}P_{\ell}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)-\text{\rm tr}\big(P_{k}\mathbf{a}P_{\ell}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)\!\Big)
=∑k≥ℓrp,k​rp^,ℓ​(tr​(Pk​Pℓ​𝐚𝐚†)−tr​(Pk​𝐚​Pℓ​𝐚†))+∑k<ℓrp,k​rp^,ℓ​(tr​(Pk​Pℓ​𝐚𝐚†)−tr​(Pk​𝐚​Pℓ​𝐚†))\displaystyle=\sum_{k\geq\ell}r_{p,k}\,r_{\hat{p},\ell}\Big(\!\text{\rm tr}\big(P_{k}P_{\ell}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)-\text{\rm tr}\big(P_{k}\mathbf{a}P_{\ell}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)\!\Big)+\sum_{k<\ell}r_{p,k}\,r_{\hat{p},\ell}\Big(\!\text{\rm tr}\big(P_{k}P_{\ell}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)-\text{\rm tr}\big(P_{k}\mathbf{a}P_{\ell}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)\!\Big)
=∑k≥ℓrp,k​rp^,ℓ​(tr​(Pℓ​𝐚𝐚†)−tr​(Pk​𝐚​Pℓ​𝐚†))+∑k<ℓrp,k​rp^,ℓ​(tr​(Pk​𝐚𝐚†)−tr​(Pk​𝐚​Pℓ​𝐚†))\displaystyle=\sum_{k\geq\ell}r_{p,k}\,r_{\hat{p},\ell}\Big(\!\text{\rm tr}\big(P_{\ell}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)-\text{\rm tr}\big(P_{k}\mathbf{a}P_{\ell}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)\!\Big)+\sum_{k<\ell}r_{p,k}\,r_{\hat{p},\ell}\Big(\!\text{\rm tr}\big(P_{k}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)-\text{\rm tr}\big(P_{k}\mathbf{a}P_{\ell}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)\!\Big)
≥∑k≥ℓrp,k​rp^,ℓ​(tr​(Pℓ​𝐚𝐚†)−tr​(𝐚​Pℓ​𝐚†))+∑k<ℓrp,k​rp^,ℓ​(tr​(Pk​𝐚𝐚†)−tr​(Pk​𝐚𝐚†)),\displaystyle\geq\sum_{k\geq\ell}r_{p,k}\,r_{\hat{p},\ell}\Big(\!\text{\rm tr}\big(P_{\ell}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)-\text{\rm tr}\big(\mathbf{a}P_{\ell}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)\!\Big)+\sum_{k<\ell}r_{p,k}\,r_{\hat{p},\ell}\Big(\!\text{\rm tr}\big(P_{k}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)-\text{\rm tr}\big(P_{k}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)\!\Big),

where in the last inequality we use Pk,Pℓ⪯IP_{k},P_{\ell}\preceq I. Thus, using the commutation relation [𝐚,𝐚†]=1[\mathbf{a},\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}]=1, we get

Similarly, if k<ℓk<\ell, then the support of 𝐚†​Πk​𝐚\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\Pi_{k}\mathbf{a} is inside the support of Πℓ\Pi_{\ell}, which implies tr​(Πk​𝐚​Πℓ​𝐚†)=tr​(𝐚†​Πk​𝐚​Πℓ)=tr​(Πk​𝐚𝐚†)\text{\rm tr}\big(\Pi_{k}\mathbf{a}\Pi_{\ell}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big)=\text{\rm tr}\big(\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\Pi_{k}\mathbf{a}\Pi_{\ell}\big)=\text{\rm tr}\big(\Pi_{k}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\big). Therefore, we have

⟨ℒ0​(ρ1/p),ρ1/p^⟩≥∑k≥ℓrp,k​rp^,ℓ​(k+1)=⟨ℒ0​(ρ^1/p),ρ^1/p^⟩.\displaystyle\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{0}\big(\rho^{1/p}\big),\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle\geq\sum_{k\geq\ell}r_{p,k}\,r_{\hat{p},\ell}(k+1)=\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{0}\big(\widehat{\rho}^{1/p}\big),\widehat{\rho}^{1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle. (23)

By using the same argument, we also have

⟨ℒ1​(ρ1/p),ρ1/p^⟩≥⟨ℒ1​(ρ^1/p),ρ^1/p^⟩.\displaystyle\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{1}\big(\rho^{1/p}\big),\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle\geq\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{1}\big(\widehat{\rho}^{1/p}\big),\widehat{\rho}^{1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle. (24)

Putting (21)-(24) together and using the fact that ν0,ν1,ω≥0\nu_{0},\nu_{1},\omega\geq 0 we conclude that Υ⁡(ρ)≥Υ⁡(ρ^)\Upsilon(\rho)\geq\Upsilon(\widehat{\rho}) for p>1p>1. The same inequality for p=1p=1 is obtained by taking the limit p→1+p\to 1^{+}. Therefore, to prove Υ⁡(ρ)≥ηth\Upsilon(\rho)\geq\eta_{\text{\rm{th}}} in Theorem 1, it suffices to restrict to diagonal states in the Fock basis.

(ii) We now, in the second step, show that the optimal diagonal states that minimize Υ⁡(ρ)\Upsilon(\rho) are thermal. Let

ρ=∑nλn​|n⟩​⟨n|,\rho=\sum_{n}\lambda_{n}|n\rangle\langle n|,

be the eigen-decomposition of ρ\rho. A straightforward computation yields

Υ⁡(ρ)\displaystyle\Upsilon(\rho) =p^​∑n(ν0​(n+1)​(λn−λn1/p​λn+11/p^)+ν1​n​(λn−λn1/p​λn−11/p^))\displaystyle=\hat{p}\sum_{n}\Big(\nu_{0}(n+1)\Big(\lambda_{n}-\lambda_{n}^{1/p}\lambda_{n+1}^{1/\hat{p}}\Big)+\nu_{1}n\Big(\lambda_{n}-\lambda_{n}^{1/p}\lambda_{n-1}^{1/\hat{p}}\Big)\!\Big)
+ω∑nnλn−∑nλnlogλn.\displaystyle\quad~+\omega\sum_{n}n\,\lambda_{n}-\sum_{n}\lambda_{n}\log\lambda_{n}. (25)

By the definition of ηth\eta_{\text{\rm{th}}} in (19), for any 0≤x≤10\leq x\leq 1 we have88 8 Here, we take the limits x→0+x\to 0^{+} and x→1−x\to 1^{-} to include the boundary values.

ηth​(1−x)≤p^​(ν0​(1−x1/p^)+ν1​(x−x1/p))+ω​x−x​log⁡x−(1−x)​log⁡(1−x).\eta_{\text{\rm{th}}}(1-x)\leq\hat{p}\Big(\nu_{0}(1-x^{1/\hat{p}})+\nu_{1}(x-x^{1/p})\Big)+\omega x-x\log x-(1-x)\log(1-x).

For any ℓ≥0\ell\geq 0 let

sℓ=∑n=ℓ∞λn,xℓ=sℓ+1sℓ.s_{\ell}=\sum_{n=\ell}^{\infty}\lambda_{n},\qquad x_{\ell}=\frac{s_{\ell+1}}{s_{\ell}}.

We note that sℓ=λℓ+sℓ+1s_{\ell}=\lambda_{\ell}+s_{\ell+1} and 0≤xℓ≤10\leq x_{\ell}\leq 1. Therefore,

ηth​(1−xℓ)≤p^​(ν0​(1−xℓ1/p^)+ν1​(x−xℓ1/p))+ω​xℓ−xℓ​log⁡xℓ−(1−xℓ)​log⁡(1−xℓ).\displaystyle\eta_{\text{\rm{th}}}(1-x_{\ell})\leq\hat{p}\Big(\nu_{0}\Big(1-x_{\ell}^{1/\hat{p}}\Big)+\nu_{1}\Big(x-x_{\ell}^{1/p}\Big)\!\Big)+\omega x_{\ell}-x_{\ell}\log x_{\ell}-(1-x_{\ell})\log(1-x_{\ell}).

Multiplying both sides by sℓs_{\ell} and summing over ℓ\ell, we obtain

ηth​∑ℓ=0∞sℓ​(1−xℓ)\displaystyle\eta_{\text{\rm{th}}}\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}s_{\ell}(1-x_{\ell}) ≤p^​∑ℓ=0∞sℓ​(ν0​(1−xℓ1/p^)+ν1​(xℓ−xℓ1/p))\displaystyle\leq\hat{p}\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}s_{\ell}\Big(\nu_{0}\Big(1-x_{\ell}^{1/\hat{p}}\Big)+\nu_{1}\Big(x_{\ell}-x_{\ell}^{1/p}\Big)\!\Big)
+ω∑ℓ=0∞sℓxℓ−∑ℓ=0∞sℓ(xℓlogxℓ+(1−xℓ)log(1−xℓ)).\displaystyle\quad~+\omega\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}s_{\ell}x_{\ell}-\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}s_{\ell}\big(x_{\ell}\log x_{\ell}+(1-x_{\ell})\log(1-x_{\ell})\big). (26)

We compute and estimate each term in the above equation as follows. First, we have

∑ℓ=0∞sℓ​(1−xℓ)=∑ℓ=0∞λℓ=1.\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}s_{\ell}(1-x_{\ell})=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\lambda_{\ell}=1.

Second, by applying Hölder’s inequality, we obtain

∑ℓ=0∞sℓ​(1−xℓ1/p^)\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}s_{\ell}(1-x_{\ell}^{1/\hat{p}}) =∑ℓ=0∞sℓ−∑ℓ=0∞sℓ1/p​sℓ+11/p^\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}s_{\ell}-\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}s_{\ell}^{1/p}s_{\ell+1}^{1/\hat{p}}
=∑ℓ=0∞sℓ−∑ℓ=0∞(∑n=ℓ∞λn)1/p​(∑n=ℓ∞λn+1)1/p^\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}s_{\ell}-\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\Big(\sum_{n=\ell}^{\infty}\lambda_{n}\Big)^{\!1/p}\Big(\sum_{n=\ell}^{\infty}\lambda_{n+1}\Big)^{\!1/\hat{p}}
≤∑ℓ=0∞∑n=ℓ∞λn−∑ℓ=0∞∑n=ℓ∞λn1/p​λn+11/p^\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\sum_{n=\ell}^{\infty}\lambda_{n}-\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\sum_{n=\ell}^{\infty}\lambda_{n}^{1/p}\lambda_{n+1}^{1/\hat{p}}
=∑n=0∞(n+1)​(λn−λn1/p​λn+11/p^).\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(n+1)\Big(\lambda_{n}-\lambda_{n}^{1/p}\lambda_{n+1}^{1/\hat{p}}\Big). (27)

Similarly, we obtain

∑ℓ=0∞sℓ​(xℓ−xℓ1/p)≤∑n=0∞n⁡(λn−λn1/p​λn−11/p^).\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}s_{\ell}(x_{\ell}-x_{\ell}^{1/p})\leq\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n\big(\lambda_{n}-\lambda_{n}^{1/p}\lambda_{n-1}^{1/\hat{p}}\big).

We also have

∑ℓ=0∞sℓ​xℓ=∑ℓ=0∞sℓ+1=∑ℓ=0∞∑n=ℓ+1∞λn=∑n=0∞n​λn.\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}s_{\ell}x_{\ell}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}s_{\ell+1}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\sum_{n=\ell+1}^{\infty}\lambda_{n}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n\lambda_{n}.

Finally, the last term of (26) becomes

∑ℓ=0∞sℓ​(xℓ​log⁡xℓ+(1−xℓ)​log⁡(1−xℓ))\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}s_{\ell}\big(x_{\ell}\log x_{\ell}+(1-x_{\ell})\log(1-x_{\ell})\big) =∑ℓ=0∞sℓ​(sℓ+1sℓ​log⁡sℓ+1sℓ+λℓsℓ​log⁡λℓsℓ)\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}s_{\ell}\Big(\frac{s_{\ell+1}}{s_{\ell}}\log\frac{s_{\ell+1}}{s_{\ell}}+\frac{\lambda_{\ell}}{s_{\ell}}\log\frac{\lambda_{\ell}}{s_{\ell}}\Big)
=∑ℓ=0∞(sℓ+1​log​sℓ+1−sℓ+1​log​sℓ+λℓ​log​λℓ−λℓ​log​sℓ)\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\Big(s_{\ell+1}\log s_{\ell+1}-s_{\ell+1}\log s_{\ell}+\lambda_{\ell}\log\lambda_{\ell}-\lambda_{\ell}\log s_{\ell}\Big)
=∑ℓ=0∞(sℓ+1​log⁡sℓ+1−sℓ​log⁡sℓ+λℓ​log⁡λℓ)\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\Big(s_{\ell+1}\log s_{\ell+1}-s_{\ell}\log s_{\ell}+\lambda_{\ell}\log\lambda_{\ell}\Big)
=∑ℓ=0∞λℓ​log⁡λℓ+limk→+∞∑ℓ=0k−1(sℓ+1​log⁡sℓ+1−sℓ​log⁡sℓ)\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\lambda_{\ell}\log\lambda_{\ell}+\lim_{k\to+\infty}\sum_{\ell=0}^{k-1}\Big(s_{\ell+1}\log s_{\ell+1}-s_{\ell}\log s_{\ell}\Big)
=∑ℓ=0∞λℓ​log⁡λℓ−s0​log⁡s0+limk→+∞sk​log⁡sk\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\lambda_{\ell}\log\lambda_{\ell}-s_{0}\log s_{0}+\lim_{k\to+\infty}s_{k}\log s_{k}
=∑ℓ=0∞λℓ​log⁡λℓ,\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\lambda_{\ell}\log\lambda_{\ell},

where in the last line we use s0=∑nλn=1s_{0}=\sum_{n}\lambda_{n}=1 and limk→+∞sk=0\lim_{k\to+\infty}s_{k}=0. Using these equations in (26) and comparing to (25) we arrive at Υ⁡(ρ)≥ηth\Upsilon(\rho)\geq\eta_{\text{\rm{th}}}.

The proof for p=1p=1 is similar; we only need to replace the Hölder inequality in (27) with

−sℓ​log⁡xℓ≤∑n=ℓ∞λn​(log⁡λn−log⁡λn+1),-s_{\ell}\log x_{\ell}\leq\sum_{n=\ell}^{\infty}\lambda_{n}\big(\log\lambda_{n}-\log\lambda_{n+1}\big),

that is derived from Hölder’s inequality by taking an appropriate limit.99 9 This inequality can also be derived from the non-negativity of the Kullback-Leibler divergence. ∎

We remark that in part (ii) of the above proof, when the diagonal state ρ\rho is thermal, the parameter xℓx_{\ell} is independent of ℓ\ell. Moreover, in this case, the Hölder inequality applied in (27) is tight.

Note that our meta log-Sobolev inequality can be viewed as a generalization of a log-sobolev inequality introduced in [17, Theorem 3.1] which holds only for the generator of the quantum-limited attenuator channel.

3.1 Meta log-Sobolev inequality for multimode states

For some applications it is useful to consider the function Υ⁡(⋅)\Upsilon(\cdot) in the multimode case and prove a generalization of Theorem 1 for multimode quantum states. In this subsection, we establish such a generalization but for the special cases of multimode states that can be prepared by applying a Gaussian unitary on multimode states that are diagonal in the Fock basis, which include all multimode Gaussian states, and multimode states that can be prepared by applying a passive Gaussian unitary on any product state.

For any mm-mode quantum state ρ\rho with finite mean photon number define

Υm​(ρ)\displaystyle\Upsilon_{m}(\rho) :=p^m​∑j=1m⟨ℒj​(ρ1/p),ρ1/p^⟩+ωm​∑j=1mtr​(ρ​𝐚j†​𝐚j)+1m​S​(ρ),\displaystyle:=\frac{\hat{p}}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{j}\big(\rho^{1/p}\big),\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle+\frac{\omega}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\text{\rm tr}(\rho\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j})+\frac{1}{m}S(\rho), (28)

where as before ν0,ν1,ω≥0\nu_{0},\nu_{1},\omega\geq 0 and ℒj=ν0​ℒ0,j+ν1​ℒ1,j\mathcal{L}_{j}=\nu_{0}\mathcal{L}_{0,j}+\nu_{1}\mathcal{L}_{1,j} is the Lindbladian acting on the jj-th mode. Note that we still use Υ⁡(ρ)=Υ1​(ρ)\Upsilon(\rho)=\Upsilon_{1}(\rho) for the single-mode case. To establish our results on the mm-mode generalizations of Theorem 1 we first state a lemma.

Lemma 2.

For any mm-mode state ρ\rho the followings hold:

  1. (i)

    Let ρ′=Dξ​ρ​Dξ†\rho^{\prime}=D_{\xi}\rho D_{\xi}^{\dagger} where Dξ=Dξ1⊗⋯⊗DξmD_{\xi}=D_{\xi_{1}}\otimes\dots\otimes D_{\xi_{m}} is an mm-mode displacement operator. Suppose that tr​(ρ​𝐚j)=0\text{\rm tr}(\rho\mathbf{a}_{j})=0 for all jj. Then, Υm​(ρ′)≥Υm​(ρ)\Upsilon_{m}(\rho^{\prime})\geq\Upsilon_{m}(\rho).

  2. (ii)

    Let ρ′=U​ρ​U†\rho^{\prime}=U\rho U^{\dagger} where UU is a passive transformation, i.e., UU is a Gaussian unitary that commutes with Hm=∑j𝐚j†​𝐚jH_{m}=\sum_{j}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j}. Then, Υm​(ρ′)=Υm​(ρ)\Upsilon_{m}(\rho^{\prime})=\Upsilon_{m}(\rho).

  3. (iii)

    Let ρ′=Sr​ρ​Sr†\rho^{\prime}=S_{r}\rho S_{r}^{\dagger} where Sr=e12​∑jrj​(𝐚j2−(𝐚j†)2)S_{r}=e^{\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j}r_{j}(\mathbf{a}_{j}^{2}-(\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger})^{2})} is a squeezing transformation. Suppose that tr​(ρ​𝐚j2)=tr​(ρ1/p​𝐚j​ρ1/p^​𝐚j)=0\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\mathbf{a}_{j}^{2}\big)=\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho^{1/p}\mathbf{a}_{j}\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\mathbf{a}_{j}\big)=0 for all jj. Then, Υm​(ρ′)≥Υm​(ρ)\Upsilon_{m}(\rho^{\prime})\geq\Upsilon_{m}(\rho).

Proof.

(i) We note that Dξ†​𝐚j​Dξ=𝐚j+ξjD_{\xi}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j}D_{\xi}=\mathbf{a}_{j}+\xi_{j}. Therefore, Dξ†​𝐚j†​𝐚j​Dξ=𝐚j†​𝐚j+ξj​𝐚j†+ξ¯j​𝐚j+|ξj|2D_{\xi}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j}D_{\xi}=\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j}+\xi_{j}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}+\bar{\xi}_{j}\mathbf{a}_{j}+|\xi_{j}|^{2}. Moreover,

tr​(ρ′​𝐚j†​𝐚j)=tr​(ρ​Dξ†​𝐚j†​𝐚k​Dξ)=tr​(ρ​𝐚j†​𝐚j)+|ξj|2,\text{\rm tr}(\rho^{\prime}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j})=\text{\rm tr}(\rho D_{\xi}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{k}D_{\xi})=\text{\rm tr}(\rho\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j})+|\xi_{j}|^{2},

where for the second equality we use the assumption tr​(ρ​𝐚j)=0\text{\rm tr}(\rho\mathbf{a}_{j})=0. We similarly have

tr​(ρ′1/p​𝐚j​ρ′1/p^​𝐚j†)=tr​(ρ1/p​𝐚j​ρ1/p^​𝐚j†)+|ξj|2.\text{\rm tr}\big({\rho^{\prime}}^{1/p}\mathbf{a}_{j}{\rho^{\prime}}^{1/\hat{p}}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\big)=\text{\rm tr}\big({\rho}^{1/p}\mathbf{a}_{j}{\rho}^{1/\hat{p}}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\big)+|\xi_{j}|^{2}.

Therefore, we have

⟨ℒ0,j​(ρ′1/p),ρ′1/p^⟩=tr​(ρ′​𝐚j​𝐚j†)−tr​(ρ′1/p​𝐚j​ρ′1/p^​𝐚j†)=⟨ℒ0,j​(ρ1/p),ρ1/p^⟩.\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{0,j}(\rho^{\prime 1/p}),\rho^{\prime 1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle=\text{\rm tr}(\rho^{\prime}\mathbf{a}_{j}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger})-\text{\rm tr}\big({\rho^{\prime}}^{1/p}\mathbf{a}_{j}{\rho^{\prime}}^{1/\hat{p}}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\big)=\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{0,j}(\rho^{1/p}),\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle.

By using similar computations, we can also show that ⟨ℒ1,j​(ρ′1/p),ρ′1/p^⟩=⟨ℒ1,j​(ρ1/p),ρ1/p^⟩\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{1,j}(\rho^{\prime 1/p}),\rho^{\prime 1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle=\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{1,j}(\rho^{1/p}),\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle. On the other hand, S⁡(ρ′)=S⁡(Dξ​ρ​Dξ†)=S⁡(ρ)S(\rho^{\prime})=S(D_{\xi}\rho D_{\xi}^{\dagger})=S(\rho). Putting these together, we find that

Υm​(ρ′)=Υm​(ρ)+ωm​∑j|ξj|2≥Υm​(ρ).\Upsilon_{m}(\rho^{\prime})=\Upsilon_{m}(\rho)+\frac{\omega}{m}\sum_{j}|\xi_{j}|^{2}\geq\Upsilon_{m}(\rho).

(ii) For any passive transformation UU, there is an m×mm\times m unitary matrix (uj​k)j,k(u_{jk})_{j,k} such that U†​𝐚j​U=∑kuj​k​𝐚kU^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j}U=\sum_{k}u_{jk}\mathbf{a}_{k}. Employing this relation yields

∑j=1mtr​(ρ′​𝐚j†​𝐚j)=∑j=1mtr​(ρ​U†​𝐚j†​U​U†​𝐚j​U)=∑j,k,k′=1muj​k​u¯j​k′​tr​(ρ​𝐚k†​𝐚k′)=∑k=1mtr​(ρ​𝐚k†​𝐚k),\sum_{j=1}^{m}\text{\rm tr}(\rho^{\prime}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j})=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\,U^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}UU^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j}U\big)=\sum_{j,k,k^{\prime}=1}^{m}u_{jk}\bar{u}_{jk^{\prime}}\,\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\mathbf{a}_{k}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{k^{\prime}}\big)=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\text{\rm tr}(\rho\mathbf{a}_{k}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{k}),

where we used ∑juj​k​u¯j​k′=δk,k′\sum_{j}u_{jk}\bar{u}_{jk^{\prime}}=\delta_{k,k^{\prime}}. Applying similar computations, one can also verify that ⟨ℒb,j​(ρ′1/p),ρ′1/p^⟩=⟨ℒb,j​(ρ1/p),ρ1/p^⟩\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{b,j}(\rho^{\prime 1/p}),\rho^{\prime 1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle=\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{b,j}(\rho^{1/p}),\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle for b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}. Therefore, using these relations together with S⁡(ρ′)=S⁡(ρ)S(\rho^{\prime})=S(\rho), we obtain Υm​(ρ′)=Υm​(ρ)\Upsilon_{m}(\rho^{\prime})=\Upsilon_{m}(\rho).

(iii) The proof of this part is more involved. First, we note that Sr†​𝐚j​Sr=cosh⁡(rj)​𝐚j−sinh⁡(rj)​𝐚j†S_{r}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j}S_{r}=\cosh(r_{j})\mathbf{a}_{j}-\sinh(r_{j})\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}, which using cosh2⁡(rj)−sinh2⁡(rj)=1\cosh^{2}(r_{j})-\sinh^{2}(r_{j})=1 implies

Sr†​𝐚j†​𝐚j​Sr=𝐚j†​𝐚j+sinh2⁡(rj)​(𝐚j†​𝐚j+𝐚j​𝐚j†)−cosh⁡(rj)​sinh⁡(rj)​((𝐚j†)2+𝐚j2).\displaystyle S_{r}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j}S_{r}=\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j}+\sinh^{2}(r_{j})(\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j}+\mathbf{a}_{j}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger})-\cosh(r_{j})\sinh(r_{j})\big((\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger})^{2}+\mathbf{a}_{j}^{2}\big). (29)

Using these relations and applying the assumption on ρ\rho, we find that

⟨ℒ0,j​(ρ′1/p),ρ′1/p^⟩\displaystyle\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{0,j}\big(\rho^{\prime 1/p}\big),\rho^{\prime 1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle =⟨ℒ0,j​(ρ1/p),ρ1/p^⟩\displaystyle=\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{0,j}\big(\rho^{1/p}\big),\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle
+sinh2⁡(rj)​(tr​(ρ​𝐚j†​𝐚j)+tr​(ρ​𝐚j​𝐚j†)−tr​(ρ1/p​𝐚j​ρ1/p^​𝐚j†)−tr​(ρ1/p​𝐚j†​ρ1/p^​𝐚j)).\displaystyle\quad\,+\sinh^{2}(r_{j})\Big(\text{\rm tr}(\rho\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j})+\text{\rm tr}(\rho\mathbf{a}_{j}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger})-\text{\rm tr}(\rho^{1/p}\mathbf{a}_{j}\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger})-\text{\rm tr}(\rho^{1/p}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\mathbf{a}_{j})\Big).

Let ρ=∑kλk​|ψk⟩​⟨ψk|\rho=\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}|\psi_{k}\rangle\langle\psi_{k}| be the eigen-decomposition of ρ\rho. Then, by Young’s inequality we have

tr​(ρ1/p​𝐚j​ρ1/p^​𝐚j†)+\displaystyle\text{\rm tr}(\rho^{1/p}\mathbf{a}_{j}\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger})+ tr​(ρ1/p​𝐚j†​ρ1/p^​𝐚j)\displaystyle\text{\rm tr}(\rho^{1/p}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\mathbf{a}_{j})
=∑k,ℓ(λk1/p​λℓ1/p^+λk1/p^​λℓ1/p)​|⟨ψk|𝐚j|ψℓ⟩|2\displaystyle=\sum_{k,\ell}\Big(\lambda_{k}^{1/p}\lambda_{\ell}^{1/\hat{p}}+\lambda_{k}^{1/\hat{p}}\lambda_{\ell}^{1/p}\Big)\big|\langle\psi_{k}|\mathbf{a}_{j}|\psi_{\ell}\rangle\big|^{2}
≥∑k,ℓ(1p​λk+1p^​λℓ+1p^​λk+1p​λℓ)​|⟨ψk|𝐚j|ψℓ⟩|2\displaystyle\geq\sum_{k,\ell}\Big(\frac{1}{p}\lambda_{k}+\frac{1}{\hat{p}}\lambda_{\ell}+\frac{1}{\hat{p}}\lambda_{k}+\frac{1}{p}\lambda_{\ell}\Big)\big|\langle\psi_{k}|\mathbf{a}_{j}|\psi_{\ell}\rangle\big|^{2}
=∑k,ℓ(λk+λℓ)​|⟨ψk|𝐚j|ψℓ⟩|2\displaystyle=\sum_{k,\ell}\big(\lambda_{k}+\lambda_{\ell}\big)\big|\langle\psi_{k}|\mathbf{a}_{j}|\psi_{\ell}\rangle\big|^{2}
=∑kλk​‖𝐚j†​|ψk⟩‖2+∑ℓλℓ​‖𝐚j​|ψℓ⟩‖2\displaystyle=\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}\big\|\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}|\psi_{k}\rangle\big\|^{2}+\sum_{\ell}\lambda_{\ell}\big\|\mathbf{a}_{j}|\psi_{\ell}\rangle\big\|^{2}
=tr​(ρ​𝐚j​𝐚j†)+tr​(ρ​𝐚j†​𝐚j).\displaystyle=\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\mathbf{a}_{j}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\big)+\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j}\big).

Therefore, we can see that

⟨ℒ0,j​(ρ′1/p),ρ′1/p^⟩≥⟨ℒ0,j​(ρ1/p),ρ1/p^⟩,\displaystyle\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{0,j}\big(\rho^{\prime 1/p}\big),\rho^{\prime 1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle\geq\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{0,j}\big(\rho^{1/p}\big),\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle,

and similarly ⟨ℒ1,j​(ρ′1/p),ρ′1/p^⟩≥⟨ℒ1,j​(ρ1/p),ρ1/p^⟩\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{1,j}\big(\rho^{\prime 1/p}\big),\rho^{\prime 1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle\geq\big\langle\mathcal{L}_{1,j}\big(\rho^{1/p}\big),\rho^{1/\hat{p}}\big\rangle. Moreover, once again using (29) we have

Notice that Theorem 3 implies Υm​(ρ)≥ηth\Upsilon_{m}(\rho)\geq\eta_{\text{\rm{th}}} for all multimode Gaussian states. The point is that by Williamson’s theorem any Gaussian state can be transformed into a tensor product of thermal states using a Gaussian unitary, and thermal states are diagonal in the Fock basis [41].

4 Log-Sobolev inequalities for the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup

As discussed in Section 2, the semigroup of attenuator channels is sometimes called the quantum (bosonic) Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup.1010 10 The quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup restricted to a certain subspace of operators resembles the classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup [9, Equation (7.5)]. In this section, we explicitly compute the optimal pp-log-Sobolev constant for this semigroup for any 1≤p≤21\leq p\leq 2, and derive a quantum variant of the celebrated log-Sobolev inequality of Gross [25]. Due to the equivalence of log-Sobolev inequalities and hypercontractivity inequalities for quantum Markov semigroups [39, 35, 2], our results provide the optimal hypercontractivity inequalities for the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup.

We need to develop some notations to present our results. Let Φt=e−t​ℒ\Phi_{t}=e^{-t\mathcal{L}} be the quantum attenuator channel with

ℒ(ρ)=e−β/2(12{𝐚𝐚†,ρ}−𝐚†ρ𝐚)+eβ/2(12{𝐚†𝐚,ρ}−𝐚ρ𝐚†),\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\rho)=e^{-\beta/2}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\big\{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},\rho\big\}-\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\rho\mathbf{a}\Big)+e^{\beta/2}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\big\{\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a},\rho\big\}-\mathbf{a}\rho\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\Big), (31)

where β>0\beta>0 is some parameter. The adjoint of the channel with respect to the Hilbert-Schmdit inner product is denoted by Φt∗\Phi_{t}^{*} and describes the evolution in the Heisenberg picture. Then, Φt∗=e−t​ℒ∗\Phi_{t}^{*}=e^{-t\mathcal{L}^{*}} where1111 11 In the literature of log-Sobolev inequalities usually ℒ\mathcal{L} is the generator in the Heisenberg picture and ℒ∗\mathcal{L}^{*} is the generator in the Schrödinger picture. Here, we change the notation since we started with channels in the Schrödinger picture in previous sections.

ℒ∗(X)=e−β/2(12{𝐚𝐚†,X}−𝐚X𝐚†)+eβ/2(12{𝐚†𝐚,X}−𝐚†X𝐚).\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{*}(X)=e^{-\beta/2}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\big\{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\dagger},X\big\}-\mathbf{a}X\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\Big)+e^{\beta/2}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\big\{\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a},X\big\}-\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}X\mathbf{a}\Big).

The semigroup {Φt:t≥0}\{\Phi_{t}:\,t\geq 0\} has a fixed point which we denote by σ=σβ\sigma=\sigma_{\beta}:

σ=σβ=(1−e−β)​∑n=0∞e−β​n​|n⟩​⟨n|.\displaystyle\sigma=\sigma_{\beta}=(1-e^{-\beta})\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta n}|n\rangle\langle n|.

Then, it is natural to define a weighted inner product with respect to this state:

⟨X,Y⟩σ=tr​(σ1/2​X†​σ1/2​Y)=⟨Γσ​(X),Y⟩,\displaystyle\langle X,Y\rangle_{\sigma}=\text{\rm tr}\big(\sigma^{1/2}X^{\dagger}\sigma^{1/2}Y\big)=\big\langle\Gamma_{\sigma}(X),Y\big\rangle, (32)

where

Γσ​(X)=σ1/2​X​σ1/2.\Gamma_{\sigma}(X)=\sigma^{1/2}X\sigma^{1/2}.

We emphasize that the weighted inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩σ\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\sigma} should not be confused with the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle that has no subscript. This inner product induces the 22-norm

‖X‖2,σ2=tr​(|Γσ1/2​(X)|2)=tr​(|σ1/4​X​σ1/4|2),\|X\|_{2,\sigma}^{2}=\text{\rm tr}\big(\big|\Gamma_{\sigma}^{1/2}(X)\big|^{2}\big)=\text{\rm tr}\big(|\sigma^{1/4}X\sigma^{1/4}|^{2}\big),

where |Y|=Y†​Y|Y|=\sqrt{Y^{\dagger}Y}. It can be verified that ℒ=Γσ∘ℒ∗∘Γσ−1\mathcal{L}=\Gamma_{\sigma}\circ\mathcal{L}^{*}\circ\Gamma_{\sigma}^{-1} and that ℒ∗\mathcal{L}^{*} is self-adjoint with respect to this weighted inner product. Thus, we may consider the Dirichlet form associated to ℒ∗\mathcal{L}^{*} given by

ℰp​(ρ)=p​p^4​⟨Γσ−1p^​(ρ1p^),ℒ∗∘Γσ−1p​(ρ1p)⟩σ.\mathcal{E}_{p}(\rho)=\frac{p\hat{p}}{4}\Big\langle\Gamma_{\sigma}^{-\frac{1}{\hat{p}}}\big(\rho^{\frac{1}{\hat{p}}}\big),\mathcal{L}^{*}\circ\Gamma_{\sigma}^{-\frac{1}{p}}\big(\rho^{\frac{1}{p}}\big)\Big\rangle_{\sigma}.

We remark that some authors define the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup by considering arbitrary parameters ν0,ν1\nu_{0},\nu_{1} satisfying ν1>ν0>0\nu_{1}>\nu_{0}>0, while here we study only the case of ν0=ν1−1=e−β/2\nu_{0}=\nu_{1}^{-1}=e^{-\beta/2}. Nevertheless, by a rescaling argument all the log-Sobolev constants of these semigroups can also be computed using Theorem 4.

Extending the definition of the weighted 22-norm, for any p≥1p\geq 1 we may define

‖X‖p,σ=tr​(|Γσ1p​(X)|p)1p.\displaystyle\|X\|_{p,\sigma}=\text{\rm tr}\Big(\Big|\Gamma_{\sigma}^{\frac{1}{p}}(X)\Big|^{p}\Big)^{\frac{1}{p}}. (37)

We let Lp​(σ)L_{p}(\sigma) to be the closure of the space of bounded operators under this norm.

The following corollary is a consequence of the above theorem, and [39, Theorem 3.8] (see also [2, Theorem 11]).

Corollary 5.

Let Φt=e−t​ℒ\Phi_{t}=e^{-t\mathcal{L}} where ℒ\mathcal{L} is given by (38). Also, let Φt∗=e−t​ℒ∗\Phi^{*}_{t}=e^{-t\mathcal{L}^{*}}. Then, for any 1<q≤p<+∞1<q\leq p<+\infty and operator X∈Lq​(σ)X\in L_{q}(\sigma) we have

‖Φt∗​(X)‖p,σ≤‖X‖q,σ,∀t≥14​α2​log⁡p−1q−1,\big\|\Phi^{*}_{t}(X)\big\|_{p,\sigma}\leq\big\|X\big\|_{q,\sigma},\qquad\quad\forall t\geq\frac{1}{4\alpha_{2}}\log\frac{p-1}{q-1},

where α2=4β​sinh2⁡(β/4)\alpha_{2}=\frac{4}{\beta}\sinh^{2}(\beta/4).

Proof.

It is well-known that it suffices restrict to operators that are positive semidefinite (see, e.g., [2]). For p≥qp\geq q define t⁡(p):=14​α2​log⁡p−1q−1t(p):=\frac{1}{4\alpha_{2}}\log\frac{p-1}{q-1} and note that t⁡(q)=0t(q)=0. For a positive semidefinite operator XX let Xp:=Φt⁡(p)∗​(X)X_{p}:=\Phi_{t(p)}^{*}(X) and define f⁡(p):=‖Xp‖p,σ−‖X‖q,σf(p):=\|X_{p}\|_{p,\sigma}-\|X\|_{q,\sigma}. Our goal is to show that f⁡(p)≤0f(p)\leq 0 for any p≥qp\geq q. To this end, since f⁡(q)=0f(q)=0, it suffices to verify that f′​(p)≤0f^{\prime}(p)\leq 0. Computing the derivative (see the details in the proof of [2, Theorem 11]) we find that

f′(p)=1p2∥Xp∥p,σp(D(ρp∥σ)−1α2ℰp(ρp)),f^{\prime}(p)=\frac{1}{p^{2}}\|X_{p}\|_{p,\sigma}^{p}\Big(D(\rho_{p}\|\sigma)-\frac{1}{\alpha_{2}}\mathcal{E}_{p}(\rho_{p})\Big),

where

ρp:=1‖Xp‖p,σp​Γσ1/p​(Xp)p.\rho_{p}:=\frac{1}{\|X_{p}\|_{p,\sigma}^{p}}\Gamma_{\sigma}^{1/p}(X_{p})^{p}.

It is shown in Appendix D that αp≥α2\alpha_{p}\geq\alpha_{2} for all pp. Then, the negativity of f′​(p)f^{\prime}(p) follows from the log-Sobolev inequality of Theorem 4.

For the above argument we need to make sure that Φt∗​(X)\Phi_{t}^{*}(X) is a well-defined operator. To this end, we notice that the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup satisfies the Feller property with respect to the algebra of compact operators [9, Theorem 5.1]. In particular, Φt∗​(X)\Phi_{t}^{*}(X) is a well-defined compact operator if XX is compact. Thus, as also done in the proof of [39, Theorem 3.8], in the above argument we may restrict to compact operators XX, and after proving the inequality for such an operator, generalize to arbitrary X∈Lq​(σ)X\in L_{q}(\sigma) by a continuity argument. We also note that since σ\sigma is Gaussian, when XX is compact and then bounded, the corresponding density operator ρp\rho_{p} in the above argument has a finite mean photon number. Thus, the log-Sobolev inequality of Theorem 4 can indeed be employed.

4.1 Log-Sobolev inequality for multimode states

It is well-known that log-Sobolev constants for classical Markov semigroups satisfy the tensorization property, meaning that for generators 𝒦1,𝒦2\mathcal{K}_{1},\mathcal{K}_{2} of two classical Markov semigroups we have αp​(𝒦1⊗I+I⊗𝒦2)=min⁡{αp​(𝒦1),αp​(𝒦2)}\alpha_{p}(\mathcal{K}_{1}\otimes I+I\otimes\mathcal{K}_{2})=\min\{\alpha_{p}(\mathcal{K}_{1}),\alpha_{p}(\mathcal{K}_{2})\}, where 𝒦1⊗ℐ+ℐ⊗𝒦2\mathcal{K}_{1}\otimes\mathcal{I}+\mathcal{I}\otimes\mathcal{K}_{2} is the generator of the tensor product semigroup {e−t​𝒦1⊗e−t​𝒦2:t≥0}\{e^{-t\mathcal{K}_{1}}\otimes e^{-t\mathcal{K}_{2}}:\,t\geq 0\}. This tensorization property is known only for some special quantum Markov semigroups; see [2] and references therein for more details. Thus, a natural question is whether the tensorization property holds for the quantum Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup. To explore this problem we first develop some notations.

For parameters β1,…,βm>0\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{m}>0 let

ℒ^=ℒ1+⋯+ℒm,\widehat{\mathcal{L}}=\mathcal{L}_{1}+\cdots+\mathcal{L}_{m},

be the generator of an mm-mode quantum Markov semigroup where

ℒj(ρ)=e−βj/2(12{𝐚j𝐚j†,ρ}−𝐚j†ρ𝐚j)+eβj/2(12{𝐚j†𝐚j,X}−𝐚jρ𝐚j†).\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{j}(\rho)=e^{-\beta_{j}/2}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\{\mathbf{a}_{j}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger},\rho\}-\mathbf{a}^{\dagger}_{j}\rho\mathbf{a}_{j}\Big)+e^{\beta_{j}/2}\Big(\frac{1}{2}\{\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j},X\}-\mathbf{a}_{j}\rho\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\Big). (38)

Then, the quantum channels

Φ^t=e−t​ℒ^=e−t​ℒ1⊗⋯⊗e−t​ℒm,\widehat{\Phi}_{t}=e^{-t\widehat{\mathcal{L}}}=e^{-t\mathcal{L}_{1}}\otimes\cdots\otimes e^{-t\mathcal{L}_{m}},

form an mm-mode semigroup. The fixed point of this semigroup is

σ^=σβ1⊗⋯⊗σβm,\widehat{\sigma}=\sigma_{\beta_{1}}\otimes\cdots\otimes\sigma_{\beta_{m}},

and its corresponding Dirichlet form is equal to

ℰp​(ρ)=p​p^4​⟨Γσ^−1p^​(ρ1p^),ℒ^∗∘Γσ^−1p​(ρ1p)⟩σ^=p​p^4​∑j=1m⟨Γσ^−1p^​(ρ1p^),ℒj∗∘Γσ^−1p​(ρ1p)⟩σ^.{\mathcal{E}}_{p}(\rho)=\frac{p\hat{p}}{4}\Big\langle\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{-\frac{1}{\hat{p}}}\big(\rho^{\frac{1}{\hat{p}}}\big),\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}\circ\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{-\frac{1}{p}}\big(\rho^{\frac{1}{p}}\big)\Big\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}}=\frac{p\hat{p}}{4}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\Big\langle\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{-\frac{1}{\hat{p}}}\big(\rho^{\frac{1}{\hat{p}}}\big),\mathcal{L}_{j}^{*}\circ\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{-\frac{1}{p}}\big(\rho^{\frac{1}{p}}\big)\Big\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}}.

Now, as in the single mode case we are interested in the pp-log-Sobolev constant

α^p=infρℰp​(ρ)D(ρ∥σ^).\widehat{\alpha}_{p}=\inf_{\rho}\frac{{\mathcal{E}}_{p}(\rho)}{D(\rho\|\widehat{\sigma})}.

Assuming that the optimal states in the above optimization problem are Gaussian, the following corollary is an evidence for the tensorization property.

Corollary 6.

Suppose that β1=⋯=βm=β\beta_{1}=\cdots=\beta_{m}=\beta. Then, for any mm-mode Gaussian state ρ\rho we have

αpD(ρ∥σ^)≤ℰ^p(ρ),\alpha_{p}D(\rho\|\widehat{\sigma})\leq\widehat{\mathcal{E}}_{p}(\rho),

where αp=p​p^4​βeβ/2(1−e−β/p)(1−e−β/p^)\alpha_{p}=\frac{p\hat{p}}{4\beta}e^{\beta/2}\big(1-e^{-\beta/p}\big)\big(1-e^{-\beta/\hat{p}}\big).

Proof.

This is a direct consequence of Theorem 3 as well as Theorem 4 and its proof.

Our next goal is to prove a lower bound on α^2\widehat{\alpha}_{2} which probably is not optimal, yet may be useful for some applications. To this end, it is useful to consider a correspondence between density operators ρ\rho and positive semidefinite operators XX as follows:

X=Γσ^−1/2(ρ1/2).X=\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{-1/2}(\rho^{1/2}).

Then, we note that ‖X‖2,σ^2=tr​(ρ)=1\|X\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}^{2}=\text{\rm tr}(\rho)=1. Indeed, Γσ^−1/2\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{-1/2} is an isometric embedding of the space of Hilbert-Schmidt operators into L2​(σ^)L_{2}(\widehat{\sigma}), the Hilbert space of operators equipped with norm ∥⋅∥2,σ^\|\cdot\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}. With this correspondence, we have

ℰ2​(ρ)=⟨X,ℒ^∗​(X)⟩σ^.\mathcal{E}_{2}(\rho)=\big\langle X,\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}(X)\big\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}}.

From this equation we realize that the spectrum of ℒ^∗\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*} is a relevant object in the study of the Dirichlet form. Here, we consider ℒ^∗\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*} as an operator acting on the Hilbert space L2​(σ^)L_{2}(\widehat{\sigma}). We note that, since σ^\widehat{\sigma} is a Gaussian state, any operator XX that is a polynomial of operators 𝐚j,𝐚j†\mathbf{a}_{j},\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger} belongs to L2​(σ^)L_{2}(\widehat{\sigma}). Letting 𝒫\mathcal{P} be the space of these polynomial operators, we find that indeed 𝒫⊂L2​(σ^)\mathcal{P}\subset L_{2}(\widehat{\sigma}) is a dense subset. Moreover, by definition, ℒ^∗\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*} leaves this subspace invariant: ℒ^∗​(𝒫)⊆𝒫\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}(\mathcal{P})\subseteq\mathcal{P}. Thus, the domain of ℒ^∗\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*} contains the dense subset 𝒫\mathcal{P} [9]. In the following proposition, we summarize Theorem 7.2 of [9] regarding the spectrum of ℒ^∗\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*} acting on L2​(σ^)L_{2}(\widehat{\sigma}), and for the sake of completeness present its main proof idea in Appendix E.1212 12 In fact in [9], the spectrum of Γσ^1/2∘ℒ^∗∘Γσ^−1/2\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{1/2}\circ\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}\circ\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{-1/2} as an operator acting on the space of Hilbert-Schmidt operators is computed.

Proposition 7.

[9] Consider ℒ^∗\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*} as an operator acting on the Hilbert space L2​(σ^)L_{2}(\widehat{\sigma}) equipped with norm ∥⋅∥2,σ^\|\cdot\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}. For z1,…,zm∈ℂz_{1},\dots,z_{m}\in\mathbb{C} with |zj|=1|z_{j}|=1 define the quadrature operator 𝐪j,zj=12​(zj​𝐚j†+z¯j​𝐚j)\mathbf{q}_{j,z_{j}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(z_{j}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}+\bar{z}_{j}\mathbf{a}_{j}). es​t−coth⁡(βj/2)4​s2=∑kj=0∞skjkj!​hj,kj​(t).\displaystyle e^{st-\frac{\coth(\beta_{j}/2)}{4}s^{2}}=\sum_{k_{j}=0}^{\infty}\frac{s^{k_{j}}}{k_{j}!}h_{j,k_{j}}(t). (39)

Then, for any tuple k=(k1,…,km)k=(k_{1},\dots,k_{m}) of non-negative integers, the operator Vk:=⨂j=1mhj,kj​(𝐪j,zj)V_{k}:=\bigotimes_{j=1}^{m}h_{j,k_{j}}(\mathbf{q}_{j,z_{j}}) is an eigenvector of ℒ^∗\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*} with eigenvalue ∑j=1msinh⁡(βj/2)​kj\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sinh(\beta_{j}/2)k_{j}. Moreover, these operators (and their appropriate linear combinations) are all the eigenvectors of ℒ^∗\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}.

For any ℓ=(ℓ1,…,ℓm)∈ℤm\ell=(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{m})\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}, let ℱℓ⊂L2​(σ^)\mathcal{F}_{\ell}\subset L_{2}(\widehat{\sigma}) be the space of operators XX such that ‖X‖2,σ^<+∞\|X\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}<+\infty and for any n=(n1,…,nm)n=(n_{1},\dots,n_{m}) their matrix entries in the Fock basis satisfy

⟨n1,…,nm​|X|​n1+ℓ1′,…,nm+ℓm′⟩=0,∀ℓ′≠ℓ.\langle n_{1},\dots,n_{m}|X|n_{1}+\ell^{\prime}_{1},\dots,n_{m}+\ell^{\prime}_{m}\rangle=0,\qquad\forall\ell^{\prime}\neq\ell.

X=∑ℓ∈ℤmXℓ,Xℓ∈ℱℓ.\displaystyle X=\sum_{\ell\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}}X_{\ell},\qquad\quad X_{\ell}\in\mathcal{F}_{\ell}. (40)

Following [6] we call (40) the diagonal decomposition of XX. A crucial property of the diagonal decomposition is that ℱℓ\mathcal{F}_{\ell}’s are orthogonal subspaces, and ⟨Xℓ,Xℓ′⟩σ^=0\langle X_{\ell},X_{\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{\widehat{\sigma}}=0 if ℓ≠ℓ′\ell\neq\ell^{\prime}. Corollary 8.

[9] For any ℓ∈ℤm\ell\in\mathbb{Z}^{m} the subspace ℱℓ\mathcal{F}_{\ell} is invariant under ℒ^∗\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}, and the eigenvalues of ℒ^∗\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*} restricted to ℱℓ\mathcal{F}_{\ell} are contained in {∑jsinh⁡(βj/2)​kj:kj≥|ℓj|}\big\{\sum_{j}\sinh(\beta_{j}/2)k_{j}:~k_{j}\geq|\ell_{j}|\big\}. (∑j=1msinh⁡(βj/2)​|ℓj|)​‖Xℓ‖2,σ^≤⟨Xℓ,ℒ^∗​(Xℓ)⟩2,σ^.\bigg(\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sinh(\beta_{j}/2)|\ell_{j}|\bigg)\|X_{\ell}\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}\leq\big\langle X_{\ell},\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*}(X_{\ell})\big\rangle_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}.

Therefore, considering the diagonal decomposition Vk=∑ℓVk,ℓV_{k}=\sum_{\ell}V_{k,\ell} of the eigenvector VkV_{k} defined in Proposition 7, we find that if Vk,ℓ≠0V_{k,\ell}\neq 0, then it is also an eigenvector of ℒ^∗\widehat{\mathcal{L}}^{*} with the same eigenvalue as that of VkV_{k}. This means that we have Vk,ℓ=0V_{k,\ell}=0 if |ℓj|>kj|\ell_{j}|>k_{j} for some jj. We also note that since by Proposition 7, the closure of the span of VkV_{k}’s is the whole space L2​(σ^)L_{2}(\widehat{\sigma}), the closure of the span of operators Vk,ℓV_{k,\ell} equals ℱℓ\mathcal{F}_{\ell}. Indeed, ℱℓ=span{Vk,ℓ:kj≥|ℓj|,∀j}¯\mathcal{F}_{\ell}=\overline{\text{span}\{V_{k,\ell}:\,k_{j}\geq|\ell_{j}|,\forall j\}}. Putting these together the desired result is implied.

To state our next lemma it is convenient to extend the definition of the entropy function for operators that are not necessarily normalized. For any positive operator X=Γσ^−1/2(ρ1/2)X=\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{-1/2}(\rho^{1/2}) where ρ\rho is a density operator, we define

Ent2,σ^(X)=D(ρ∥σ^).\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}(X)=D(\rho\|\widehat{\sigma}).

Extending this definition to non-normalized operators satisfying ‖X‖2,σ^<+∞\|X\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}<+\infty, we let

Ent2,σ^​(X)=‖X‖2,σ^2​Ent2,σ^​(X‖X‖2,σ^).\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}(X)=\|X\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}^{2}\,\text{\rm Ent}_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}\Big(\frac{X}{\|X\|_{2,\widehat{\sigma}}}\Big).

The significance of this entropy function is in its connection to the derivative of p↦‖X‖p,σ^p\mapsto\|X\|_{p,\widehat{\sigma}} at p=2p=2 for which we refer to [39, 35, 2].

Lemma 9.

Let XX be a positive operator satisfying tr​(ρ​Hm)<+∞\text{\rm tr}\big(\rho H_{m}\big)<+\infty where ρ=Γσ^1/2​(X)2\rho=\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{1/2}(X)^{2} and Hm=∑j=1m𝐚j†​𝐚jH_{m}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathbf{a}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathbf{a}_{j} is the mm-mode number operator. Then, for any vector w=(wℓ)ℓw=(w_{\ell})_{\ell} of positive real numbers we have

where XℓX_{\ell}’s are given by the diagonal decomposition X=∑ℓXℓX=\sum_{\ell}X_{\ell} with Xℓ∈ℱℓX_{\ell}\in\mathcal{F}_{\ell}. Also, I2,2(Xℓ)=Γσ^−1/2(|Γσ^1/2(Xℓ)|)I_{2,2}(X_{\ell})=\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{-1/2}\big(\big|\Gamma_{\widehat{\sigma}}^{1/2}(X_{\ell})\big|\big) and ‖w‖22=∑ℓwℓ2\|w\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{\ell}w_{\ell}^{2}.

Proof.

Fix a finite subset S⊂ℤmS\subset\mathbb{Z}^{m} satisfying −ℓ∈S-\ell\in S for all ℓ∈S\ell\in S. For some technical reason, in the following we restrict to the subspace of operators XX satisfying Xℓ=0X_{\ell}=0 if ℓ∉S\ell\notin S. Later, we will relax this assumption.

We remark that Lemma 9 holds beyond the diagonal decomposition considered above and works for any decomposition of the space of operators into orthogonal subspaces. Thus, this lemma is of independent interest and may find other applications.

5 Proof of the CMOE conjecture

In this section, we present an alternative proof of the CMOE conjecture for single-mode phase-covariant Gaussian channels, which is first established in [15, 16].

Theorem 11.

[CMOE Conjecture] For any single-mode phase-covariant Gaussian channel Φ\Phi, and any quantum state ρ\rho with finite mean photon number we have

S⁡(Φ⁡(ρ))≥S⁡(Φ⁡(τ)),\displaystyle S\big(\Phi(\rho)\big)\geq S\big(\Phi(\tau)\big), (46)

where τ\tau is a single-mode thermal state satisfying S⁡(ρ)=S⁡(τ)S(\rho)=S(\tau).

To prove this theorem we first state a consequence of Theorem 1.

Theorem 12.

Let {Φt:t≥0}\{\Phi_{t}:\,t\geq 0\} denote a semigroup of single-mode phase-covariant Gaussian channels. Then, for any α>0\alpha>0 we have

ηth​(α)=infρdd​t​S​(Φt​(ρ))|t=0+α​S​(ρ),\displaystyle\eta_{\text{\rm{th}}}(\alpha)=\inf_{\rho}\,\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}t}S\big(\Phi_{t}(\rho)\big)\Big|_{t=0}+\alpha S(\rho), (47)

where the infimum is taken over all quantum states ρ\rho with finite mean photon number, and ηth​(α)\eta_{\text{\rm{th}}}(\alpha) is the infimum of the same function restricted to thermal states.

Proof of Theorem 12.

Let ℒ\mathcal{L} be the Lindbladian of the semigroup {Φt:t≥0}\{\Phi_{t}:\,t\geq 0\} so that Φt=e−t​ℒ\Phi_{t}=e^{-t\mathcal{L}}. We have

dd​t​S​(Φt​(ρ))|t=0=⟨ℒ⁡(ρ),log⁡ρ⟩.\displaystyle\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}t}S\big(\Phi_{t}(\rho)\big)\Big|_{t=0}=\langle\mathcal{L}(\rho),\log\rho\rangle. (48)

Then, the claim follows from Theorem 1 for p=1p=1 and appropriate choices of ν0,ν1≥0\nu_{0},\nu_{1}\geq 0 and ω=0\omega=0.

∎

We need yet another technical ingredient to prove Theorem 11. For 0<x<10<x<1 let

τx=(1−x)​∑nxn​|n⟩​⟨n|,\displaystyle\tau_{x}=(1-x)\sum_{n}x^{n}|n\rangle\langle n|, (49)

be a thermal state with parameter xx. Then, letting Φt=e−t​ℒ\Phi_{t}=e^{-t\mathcal{L}} with ℒ=ν0​ℒ0+ν1​ℒ1\mathcal{L}=\nu_{0}\mathcal{L}_{0}+\nu_{1}\mathcal{L}_{1} and using (48), we find that the objective function in (47) for thermal states equals

=11−x​((ν1​x−ν0)​log⁡x−α​x​log⁡x−α⁡(1−x)​log⁡(1−x)).\displaystyle\,=\frac{1}{1-x}\Big(\!(\nu_{1}x-\nu_{0})\log x-\alpha x\log x-\alpha(1-x)\log(1-x)\!\Big).

This equation can also be derived by taking the limit of p→1+p\to 1^{+} in (18).

Assume that ν0>0\nu_{0}>0 and as before let α>0\alpha>0. Then, we have limx→0+fα​(x)=limx→1−fα​(x)=+∞\lim_{x\to 0^{+}}f_{\alpha}(x)=\lim_{x\to 1^{-}}f_{\alpha}(x)=+\infty. This means that the minimum of fα​(x)f_{\alpha}(x) is attained at roots of fα′​(x)f^{\prime}_{\alpha}(x). We have

fα′​(x)\displaystyle f^{\prime}_{\alpha}(x) =11−x​(ν1​log⁡x+ν1​x−ν0x−α​log⁡x+α​log⁡(1−x))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{1-x}\Big(\nu_{1}\log x+\frac{\nu_{1}x-\nu_{0}}{x}-\alpha\log x+\alpha\log(1-x)\Big)
+1(1−x)2​((ν1​x−ν0)​log⁡x−α​x​log⁡x−α⁡(1−x)​log⁡(1−x))\displaystyle\quad~+\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}\Big((\nu_{1}x-\nu_{0})\log x-\alpha x\log x-\alpha(1-x)\log(1-x)\Big)
=1(1−x)2​((ν1−ν0)​log⁡x+(1−x)​(ν1​x−ν0)x−α​log⁡x)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(1-x)^{2}}\bigg(\!(\nu_{1}-\nu_{0})\log x+\frac{(1-x)(\nu_{1}x-\nu_{0})}{x}-\alpha\log x\bigg)

Therefore, fα′​(x)=0f^{\prime}_{\alpha}(x)=0 iff g⁡(x)=αg(x)=\alpha where

Computing the derivative of g⁡(x)g(x), we have

Moreover, since ν0>0\nu_{0}>0 we have limx→0+g⁡(x)=+∞\lim_{x\to 0^{+}}g(x)=+\infty and limx→1−g⁡(x)=0\lim_{x\to 1^{-}}g(x)=0. This means that g⁡(x)≥0g(x)\geq 0 for all 0<x<10<x<1, and g⁡(x)g(x) takes any positive value in this interval exactly once. As a conclusion, g⁡(x)=αg(x)=\alpha has exactly one solution in (0,1)(0,1) for any α>0\alpha>0. We conclude that, if α>0\alpha>0, the minimum of fα​(x)f_{\alpha}(x) is attained at the unique root of fα′​(x)f^{\prime}_{\alpha}(x). More importantly, for any 0<x0<10<x_{0}<1, there is α0=g⁡(x0)\alpha_{0}=g(x_{0}) such that the minimum of fα0​(x)f_{\alpha_{0}}(x) is attained at x=x0x=x_{0}.

ηth​(αt)=dd​s​S​(Φs​(τxt))|s=0+αt​S​(τxt).\eta_{\text{\rm{th}}}(\alpha_{t})=\frac{\text{\rm{d}}}{\text{\rm{d}}s}S\big(\Phi_{s}(\tau_{x_{t}})\big)\big|_{s=0}+\alpha_{t}S(\tau_{x_{t}}).
